papers.citation: Tzvetan Zakharko (tzakharko), "m4-sme-exploration: Exploring the Scalable Matrix Extension of the Apple M4 processor" (reports/01-sme-overview.md, benchmarks.yaml)
papers.core_idea: The only systematic public characterization of Apple M4 SME. Establishes SVL=512 bits, ZA=4096 bytes, that M4 has no non-streaming SVE (streaming SVE is the only path to Z registers), and — critically — that the SME block is ONE UNIT PER CORE CLUSTER shared by all cores in that cluster, that a single core can already saturate it, and that M4 Pro has two P-cluster units plus a lower-throughput E-cluster unit. Reports SMOPA peak rates (~4010 GOPS i8→i32, ~2006 GOPS i16→i64).
papers.relevance: This is the single most damaging piece of prior art for the framing of our +57% co-scheduling result. Once "SME is a shared cluster coprocessor, disjoint from the per-core NEON pipes" is public, "SME threads and NEON threads add throughput" is a corollary, not a discovery. Our contribution must be re-scoped to the *quantification for a symmetric cipher*, the optimal-split finding (2 SME + 8 NEON, and that 4 SME threads is worse), and the constant-time/security analysis — not to the architectural fact. It also validates our harness: our measured SMOPA rates match this source closely.

papers.citation: Hanyu Wei, Wenqian Li, Shiyu Shen, Hao Yang, Yunlei Zhao, "Optimized Implementation of ML-KEM on ARMv9-A with SVE2 and SME"
papers.core_idea: VecNTT (SVE2) and MatNTT (SME) implementations of the ML-KEM number-theoretic transform, benchmarked on an Apple M4 Pro. Reports up to 7.18x and 7.77x over the reference implementation.
papers.relevance: This is the closest existing work and the one a reviewer will hold up first. It is the ONLY cryptography paper on ePrint that uses SME, and it is lattice/NTT — i.e. it uses the ZA matrix tiles for the workload matrix units are actually good at. It does NOT touch symmetric ciphers, does not use streaming SVE for bitwise/rotate workloads, does not use XAR, and does not study SME/NEON concurrency. Our positive result (ChaCha20 in streaming SVE) and our negative result (ZA is a net loss for 5x51 Curve25519 limbs and Poly1305) are both complementary to it and neither is covered by it. It also gives us the one citation we need for "the published win for matrix units is lattice PQC."

papers.citation: Chencheng Deng, Weiling Yang, Jianbin Fang, Dezun Dong, "Demystifying ARM SME to Optimize General Matrix Multiplications"
papers.core_idea: Architectural characterization of SME on Apple M4 Pro plus MpGEMM, an open-source GEMM library, achieving 1.23x average over Apple Accelerate on DeepSeek/LLaMA-shaped workloads. Documents per-cluster SME unit counts and per-precision SMOPA throughput.
papers.relevance: Our SMOPA measurements match its published figures, which is the cheapest way to establish harness credibility in a write-up. It also fixes the boundary of prior art: SME characterization work to date is entirely GEMM/HPC, with no crypto, no bitwise-integer workload, and no cross-unit co-scheduling study.

papers.citation: Romain Dolbeau, ChaCha20 ARM SVE implementation, SUPERCOP `crypto_stream/chacha20/dolbeau/arm-sve`
papers.venue_year: SUPERCOP / eBACS, unpublished implementation (no accompanying paper found)
papers.core_idea: VL-agnostic C+intrinsics vectorization of ChaCha20 for ARM SVE, processing a variable number of blocks per pass depending on the runtime vector length. Uses `sveor_u32_x` + `svlsl_n_u32_x` for the rotates.
papers.relevance: This is the real prior art for our claim, and it means "ChaCha20 on ARM scalable vectors" is NOT new. What is not covered: it is non-streaming SVE (unavailable on M4 at all), it predates/ignores SVE2 XAR so it spends 3 instructions per rotate where we spend 1, and it has never been run in a streaming-mode context where NEON is illegal. Our claim must be narrowed from "first scalable-vector ChaCha20" to "first ChaCha20 in Arm SME streaming mode, and first quantification of the XAR contribution." We should also benchmark against a port of this code, not only against our own NEON.

papers.citation: Ange Albertini, Thai Duong, Shay Gueron, Stefan Kölbl, Atul Luykx, Sophie Schmieg, "How to Abuse and Fix Authenticated Encryption Without Key Commitment"
papers.core_idea: Shows AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are not key-committing, builds working multi-key ciphertexts that decrypt to valid files under two keys, and gives both a generic explicit-commitment construction and a scheme-specific fix.
papers.relevance: Blindplane's "key commitment" property is precisely this construction. It is a 2022 standardized-by-now technique (see the CFRG AEAD-properties draft), so it cannot be presented as a design contribution — only as a correct choice. Cite it as the source, not as our idea.

papers.citation: Jinyuan Li, Maxwell Krohn, David Mazières, Dennis Shasha, "Secure Untrusted Data Repository (SUNDR)"
papers.core_idea: Defines fork consistency: with a fully Byzantine server, clients sign a hash-chained version structure over all operations, so a server that hides one client's write from another must fork them permanently — detectable as soon as the two clients communicate.
papers.relevance: This is the correct name and the correct prior art for Blindplane's "signed manifest hash chain head for rollback detection." It is a 22-year-old idea. Worse for us, SUNDR gets fork *consistency*; a per-client persisted head only gets per-client rollback detection and does NOT detect a relay equivocating between two different clients unless they gossip. Either add cross-client comparison / a transparency-log anchor, or state the weaker property explicitly in the README. Do not claim novelty here.

papers.citation: Ariel J. Feldman, William P. Zeller, Michael J. Freedman, Edward W. Felten, "SPORC: Group Collaboration using Untrusted Cloud Resources"
papers.core_idea: Framework for collaborative apps on an untrusted server: clients hold all keys, the server sees only ciphertext and ordering, hash chains (borrowed from BFT2F) limit equivocation, and operational transformation lets clients automatically *recover* from a malicious fork rather than only detect it.
papers.relevance: SPORC is architecturally the closest published ancestor of Blindplane's whole shape: untrusted relay that orders and stores but cannot read, clients that detect misbehaviour via hash chains. A reviewer will ask what Blindplane adds over SPORC. The honest answers are engineering ones (HPKE instead of ad-hoc envelopes, key-committing AEAD, blind indexes, a Rust crate boundary) — not a new security property.

papers.citation: Beom Heyn Kim, David Lie, "Caelus: Verifying the Consistency of Cloud Services with Battery-Powered Devices"
papers.core_idea: Makes the cloud service declare the timing and order of operations in a signed attestation log, and rotates the role of log attester among a user's personal devices to build a virtual highly-available attester, converting fork detection into near-real-time consistency verification.
papers.relevance: Directly relevant to strengthening Blindplane's freshness story. If we want the rollback claim to survive review, this is the design to borrow from: multiple client devices attesting the head, rather than one client persisting one head. Also the right citation for why "a replayed old record still verifies" is a known, solved-ish problem class.

papers.citation: Raluca Ada Popa, Catherine M. S. Redfield, Nickolai Zeldovich, Hari Balakrishnan, "CryptDB: Protecting Confidentiality with Encrypted Query Processing"
papers.core_idea: Onion encryption over SQL: data is stored encrypted, the DBMS executes queries on ciphertext by peeling to deterministic or order-preserving layers, and keys can be chained to user passwords so the DBA never obtains plaintext.
papers.relevance: The canonical "server cannot decrypt" database. Its documented failure mode — DET/OPE layers leak equality, order and frequency — is exactly the leakage profile Blindplane's scoped blind indexes have. Reviewers will map our blind index onto CryptDB's DET onion immediately. Naming the leak in the README is good practice but is not a research contribution.

papers.citation: Melissa Chase, Trevor Perrin, Greg Zaverucha, "The Signal Private Group System and Anonymous Credentials Supporting Efficient Verifiable Encryption"
papers.core_idea: Keyed-verification anonymous credentials over an algebraic MAC let a server store encrypted group-membership entries and authenticate members as "corresponding to some encrypted entry" without learning which, hiding group membership from the service provider.
papers.relevance: The state of the art for hiding the *access graph* from a server. Blindplane explicitly leaks the access graph ("which recipient identifiers can read which record, and when that changed"). This paper is the reason that leak is a design gap rather than an inherent cost, and it is what a reviewer will cite when asking why we did not do better.

papers.citation: Jeffrey C. Ching, Quan Zhou, Danfeng Zhang, "Filament: Denning-Style Information Flow Control for Rust"
papers.core_idea: Static, variable-level IFC for Rust with no compiler modification: type-inference-driven explicit-flow checking, a `pc_block!` macro for implicit flows via compile-time program-counter labels, and macros for safe interop with std. Claims a more permissive model than Cocoon with fewer escape hatches.
papers.relevance: This plus Cocoon is the published answer to "is there prior work on structural/compile-time enforcement of security properties?" — yes, and it is far stronger than ours. These systems enforce a *semantic* property (non-interference) with a stated adversary model. `cargo tree | grep` enforces the absence of a *crate name*. Claim 3 cannot be published against this baseline; it should be presented as engineering discipline, not as a technique.

papers.citation: Ada Lamba, Max Taylor, Vincent Beardsley, Jacob Bambeck, Michael D. Bond, Zhiqiang Lin, "Cocoon: Static Information Flow Control in Rust"
papers.core_idea: A Rust library that builds a type-based effect system out of the unmodified type system plus procedural macros, allowing arbitrary computation over secret values while statically preventing secret-to-public flows, with zero runtime overhead. Demonstrated by retrofitting the Spotify TUI client and Mozilla Servo.
papers.relevance: Same as Filament: it is the correct comparison point, and it shows what "structural enforcement of a security property in Rust" has to look like to be a contribution. If Blindplane ever wants a real claim here, the move is to encode "no decryption capability" as a type-level or effect-level property that composes, and prove a non-interference-flavoured statement — not to grep a dependency tree in CI.

papers.citation: Shuichi Katsumata, Kris Kwiatkowski, Federico Pintore, Thomas Prest, "Scalable Ciphertext Compression Techniques for Post-Quantum KEMs and their Applications"
papers.core_idea: Formalizes multi-recipient KEMs (mKEM) and gives compression techniques that make an N-recipient ciphertext far smaller than N independent ones (≈16x for mKyber), with an application to reducing MLS/TreeKEM group-key-agreement bandwidth.
papers.relevance: Defines the primitive Blindplane's "HPKE multi-recipient envelope" is an unoptimized instance of. Our envelope is N independent HPKE encapsulations — correct, standard, and strictly worse than the literature. Useful two ways: it forecloses a novelty claim on the envelope, and it is a concrete, citable optimization we could actually implement (and a natural PQC migration path).

papers.citation: IronCore Labs, "Cloaked Search" (product and documentation)
papers.core_idea: A transparent encryption proxy in front of Elasticsearch/OpenSearch that encrypts and tokenizes indexed fields so the search service is blind to their contents, using a distinct key per (tenant, index, field) tuple and requiring documents to be tagged with their tenant.
papers.relevance: This is our scoped blind index, in production, with essentially the same scoping tuple — we use (tenant, label, key_epoch), they use (tenant, index, field). It is the strongest single piece of evidence that Blindplane's data-plane design is a known composition rather than a new one. Any write-up must cite it and say what, if anything, differs.

papers.citation: MongoDB, "Queryable Encryption" (product documentation, GA in MongoDB 7.0)
papers.core_idea: Client-side field-level encryption with server-side equality and range query support over structured-encryption indexes; the server stores only randomized ciphertext and index metadata and cannot decrypt, including during query execution.
papers.relevance: A shipping, mainstream, server-blind, queryable data plane with a stronger query model than Blindplane's equality-only blind index. It is the commercial baseline the design will be measured against, and it means "server-blind indexed storage" is a product category, not a research gap.

papers.citation: Alexander Krause et al., "BlindexTEE: A Blind Index Approach towards TEE-supported End-to-end Encrypted DBMS"
papers.core_idea: Combines blind indexes with a TEE-backed component to build an end-to-end encrypted DBMS, explicitly using the term "blind index" as the searchable-encryption mechanism.
papers.relevance: Establishes "blind index" as current, named, published terminology in exactly our problem space, and that recent work in this area competes on either leakage bounds or TEE assumptions — two dimensions where Blindplane makes no claim. Useful mainly as evidence of how crowded the space is.

papers.citation: Alexandros Daglis et al. (as surfaced), "Occamy: Elastically Sharing a SIMD Co-processor across Multiple CPU Cores"
papers.core_idea: Architecture for a wide SIMD co-processor shared elastically among several CPU cores rather than replicated per core, with mechanisms to arbitrate and balance access.
papers.relevance: Prior art for the general architectural pattern our co-scheduling result exploits (one wide shared vector unit + per-core narrow SIMD). It means the *systems* insight is not new either; only the crypto instantiation and the measured optimum are. Cite it defensively rather than let a reviewer find it.

papers.citation: Alexander Breuer, Friedrich Schiller University Jena, "Hello SME!" documentation and "Generating Fast Matrix Multiplication Kernels Using the Scalable Matrix Extension" (arXiv:2409.18779)
papers.core_idea: Tutorial-grade documentation and microbenchmarks for SME programming, plus a code generator for SME matmul kernels. Confirms streaming SVL and instruction behaviour on Apple parts.
papers.relevance: Together with tzakharko and Deng et al., this pins down the complete public SME literature: it is entirely GEMM and HPC. Nothing in it addresses ciphers, bitwise/rotate kernels, constant-time execution, or the AESE/PMULL absence in streaming mode. This is the citation set that supports the negative claim "no prior symmetric-crypto SME work exists."

techniques.name: ChaCha20 quarter-round in SME streaming SVE with fused XAR (16 blocks/pass at SVL=512)
techniques.source: Our own measurement (docs/research/apple-acceleration-findings.json block [3], lab/b9.c); XAR-for-rotates is documented as an SVE2 idiom in zingaburga's SVE2 critique gist; Dolbeau's SUPERCOP arm-sve ChaCha20 is the non-XAR scalable-vector precedent
techniques.applies_to: ChaCha20, XChaCha20, the ChaCha half of ChaCha20-Poly1305; same shape applies to BLAKE2b and Argon2id's G function on .d lanes
techniques.expected_gain: 4.03x over our hand-written NEON on the round function: 11.50–11.90 GB/s keystream on one P-core vs 2.86–3.03 GB/s NEON; 10.63 GB/s from pure Rust with zero deps. Decomposes into ~2.15x from 512-bit lanes (net of the SME unit's lower 3.6 vs 6.7 G vec-instr/s issue rate) and ~1.87x from XAR fusing eor+shl+usra into one instruction. Caveat: keystream only, not measured as a complete AEAD.
techniques.effort: Medium-high. Roadmap item #13, currently in progress. Requires one monolithic `core::arch::asm!` block with `.arch armv9-a+sme+sme2` as the first line inside it (using -C target-feature instead makes LLVM autovectorize unrelated code with non-streaming SVE, which SIGILLs on M4), v8–v15 in the clobber list, and no compiler-inserted spills or libc calls inside the streaming region.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes, with measured support: XAR/ADD streaming loops timed 3.1823 ns/iter on all-zero operands vs 3.1580 ns/iter on random — 0.8% spread, i.e. noise. MSR DIT works inside streaming mode, so the DIT guarantee remains available. smstart/smstop zeroing the vector file is a free secret wipe. Two caveats: a mean-timing spread is not a constant-time proof (needs dudect/TIMECOP), and the SME unit is shared across the P-cluster, creating an SMT-like coarse contention channel visible to a co-resident process — key-independent for our access pattern, but it does reveal that crypto is running.

techniques.name: Heterogeneous SME+NEON co-scheduling with a tuned thread split
techniques.source: Our own measurement (lab/b10.c, b11.c); architectural basis published by tzakharko (shared per-cluster SME unit) and Deng et al. arXiv:2512.21473 (per-cluster unit counts on M4 Pro); general cooperative-split principle in EngineCL/CoopCL and Occamy
techniques.applies_to: Bulk ChaCha20/XChaCha20. Does NOT apply to AES-GCM (AESE and PMULL are unavailable in streaming mode, and NEON is illegal inside it, so the two cannot interleave in one loop).
techniques.expected_gain: +57% over the best NEON-only configuration: 2 SME + 8 NEON threads = 29.87 GB/s aggregate, vs 19.0 GB/s NEON-only at 10 threads and 21.1 GB/s SME-only at any thread count. Full sweep measured: 1+0=11.63, 0+9=19.39, 1+9=26.77, 2+8=29.87, 2+7=29.15, 3+7=27.41, 4+6=27.50, 0+10=18.99. Note the single-thread 4x advantage decays to 1.82x at 4 threads and ~1.1x at 9–10 threads because SME saturates at ~21 GB/s.
techniques.effort: Low once the SSVE kernel exists — a work-stealing queue where 2 workers take the SSVE path and the rest take NEON. The tuning is the real cost: 4 SME threads is *worse* than 2, and the optimum differs across M4 / M4 Pro / M4 Max, so the split must be probed at startup rather than hardcoded.
techniques.constant_time_safe: No new cryptographic exposure beyond the shared-SME contention channel, but it makes that channel busier and more observable. Real cost: two independent implementations of the same primitive doubles the verification surface, and a divergence between them would only manifest at specific thread counts — differential fuzzing between the SSVE and NEON paths is mandatory, not optional.

techniques.name: Streaming-mode instruction availability map and transition cost model for Apple M4
techniques.source: Our own probes (lab/b8.c, sveprobe.c, sme_test.c, fa64.c); no equivalent published anywhere found
techniques.applies_to: Every primitive in the crate — it determines what can and cannot move into streaming mode at all
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified as a speedup; this is enabling knowledge. Establishes: SVL=512 bits (sme_max_svl_b=64); M4 has NO standalone SVE (`ptrue p0.b` outside streaming mode SIGILLs); available in streaming mode: XAR, EOR3, TBL, MUL/UMULH .d; NOT available: AESE, PMULL, RAX1 (Apple does not advertise FEAT_SME_FA64); smstart/smstop round trip is 9.6 ns, negligible when chunking at >=4 KiB; smstart/smstop zeroes the entire vector register file including callee-saved v8–v15.
techniques.effort: Already done. The value is in writing it down — it is the part of the work with the clearest claim to being unpublished.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Neutral, but two security-relevant consequences fall out: (1) AES-GCM and SHA-3-family work can never move into streaming mode, so the AES path stays NEON forever; (2) xnu context-switches ZA/ZT0 via machine_save/restore_sme_context() into kernel-side thread state, so any secret left in ZA is spilled to kernel memory — sidestepped here only because the ChaCha path uses Z vectors and never ZA.

techniques.name: SME ZA outer-product (SMOPA) for Curve25519 / Poly1305 limb arithmetic — NEGATIVE RESULT
techniques.source: Our own measurement (lab/b3.c, b5.c, b6.c, rsme_src_main.rs); contrasts with the positive lattice/NTT result in ePrint 2026/093
techniques.applies_to: X25519, Ed25519 field multiply (5x51 limbs), Poly1305 130-bit modular arithmetic
techniques.expected_gain: Net loss, 5–7x SLOWER per field multiply. Raw MAC rate is a trap: 955 G int16 MAC/s (SMOPA i16→i64 at 0.268 ns/instr x 256 MACs), but a realistic kernel (load operands, zero ZA, one SMOPA, store the 8x8 i64 tile) costs 60.4 ns against ~8–13 ns for the current scalar 5x51 multiply. ZA readout is the killer: targeted ST1D from ZA runs 6.17 ns/row, so extracting one tile costs ~49 ns and swamps the 0.27 ns of actual multiply. Streaming-SVE MUL/UMULH .d avoiding ZA entirely gives 3.48 G products/s, still under scalar's 5.34–6.61 G.
techniques.effort: Already measured and refuted. Zero further effort; the value is publishing the refutation.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Moot given the verdict, but measured anyway: SMOPA timing is data-independent (0.2647 / 0.2610 / 0.2658 / 0.2683 ns for all-zeros / all-ones / random / all-0x7fff, a 2.7% spread). The would-be concern is the ZA-to-kernel-memory spill on context switch.

techniques.name: Multi-recipient KEM (mKEM) instead of N independent HPKE encapsulations
techniques.source: Katsumata, Kwiatkowski, Pintore, Prest, ASIACRYPT 2020 / ePrint 2020/1107
techniques.applies_to: blindplane-core's per-recipient HPKE envelope construction
techniques.expected_gain: Bandwidth: up to ~16x smaller than N independent ciphertexts for the lattice instantiation; for X25519-based HPKE the saving is smaller but the shared-randomness structure still removes N-1 ephemeral scalar multiplications from the seal path. Our own profiling already says the record cost is dominated by curve and signature work, not the payload AEAD, so this hits the actual bottleneck.
techniques.effort: High — it is a real protocol change with its own security analysis, and it deviates from RFC 9180's single-recipient mode, so interop with the `hpke` reference crate (currently a cross-check) would be lost for the envelope.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Orthogonal to constant time; the implementation would need the same masked-Choice discipline as the existing code. The real caveat is that mKEM has its own security model (malicious-recipient settings need care — see the Lattice-Based MMKEM with Malicious Security follow-up work), so this is not a drop-in.

techniques.name: Fork-consistency upgrade: cross-client head comparison or an attested log, replacing per-client head persistence
techniques.source: SUNDR (OSDI 2004), SPORC (OSDI 2010), Caelus (IEEE S&P 2015)
techniques.applies_to: blindplane-wire / blindplane-core rollback detection (the signed manifest hash chain)
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified as performance; it is a security-property upgrade. Today a per-client persisted head detects rollback *for that client only*; a relay can equivocate between two clients indefinitely and neither will notice. SUNDR-style version structures give fork consistency; Caelus-style rotating attesters across a user's devices gives near-real-time consistency verification.
techniques.effort: Medium for the Caelus-style multi-device head attestation; high for full SUNDR-style version structures with per-operation signed version vectors.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Not a constant-time concern — this is integrity/freshness machinery operating on public metadata.

techniques.name: Set PSTATE.DIT around field arithmetic and AEAD cores
techniques.source: Apple's own guidance for Apple Silicon; hw.optional.arm.FEAT_DIT = 1 confirmed on this M4 (our probe, lab/ct.c); currently not done anywhere in the crate
techniques.applies_to: Every secret-dependent code path: Curve25519 field arithmetic, Ed25519, Poly1305, the AEAD cores
techniques.expected_gain: No throughput gain (small overhead if anything). The gain is assurance: without DIT, data-independent timing on Apple Silicon is a microarchitectural implementation detail, not an architectural guarantee. None of the instructions we use (SHA512H/H2/SU0/SU1, EOR3/BCAX/XAR/RAX1, AESE/AESMC, PMULL, REV32, TBL, SRI/SHL) are data-dependent, so this converts an empirical claim into a documented one.
techniques.effort: Low — an MSR write around the relevant regions, plus runtime detection. Works inside streaming mode too, which we verified.
techniques.constant_time_safe: This IS the constant-time improvement. It is also the cheapest single thing that would make the library's constant-time story defensible to a reviewer, and its current absence is a gap between the README's claims and the code.

techniques.name: Cross-core SME contention as a side/covert channel — measure it rather than only note it
techniques.source: Implied by tzakharko's shared-per-cluster finding plus our own contention sweep; no published measurement of this channel found
techniques.applies_to: Threat model for the whole library on Apple Silicon, not one primitive
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified — this is a proposed experiment, not a result. The hypothesis is that a process on a sibling P-core can detect, by timing its own SME work, when another process enters streaming mode, yielding an SMT-like coarse channel across a security boundary that most people assume is not shared.
techniques.effort: Medium — a two-process contention harness plus a channel-capacity measurement in bit/s. Substantially less work than a full cipher implementation.
techniques.constant_time_safe: N/A — this is an attack-side measurement. Note it cuts against our own security story: if the channel is real, our SME ChaCha path leaks *when* crypto runs (though not key material, since our access pattern is key-independent). Reviewers would rather see us measure it than assert it is harmless.

notes:
HONEST BOTTOM LINE, up front: there is ONE paper here, and it is the SME one. Claims 2 and 3 are not publishable and should not be advanced as novel. The project as a whole is a strong engineering artifact with one genuinely unpublished measurement campaign inside it.

=== 1. SME / STREAMING-SVE FOR CRYPTOGRAPHY: WHAT I SEARCHED AND DID NOT FIND ===

Since absence of prior art is the crux, here is the exhaustive record.

SEARCHED, FOUND NOTHING:
- IACR ePrint full-text search for "Scalable Matrix Extension" — 5 results total, only 2026/093 relevant (ML-KEM NTT on M4 Pro). ePrint search for "SVE2" — exactly 2 results, 2026/093 and 2025/2208 (ML-DSA on ARMv9-A), same authors, both PQC/NTT. There is NO symmetric-cryptography SME or streaming-SVE paper on ePrint.
- arXiv: every SME paper found is GEMM/HPC — "Hello SME!" (2409.18779), "Demystifying ARM SME" (2512.21473), "LOw-cOst yet High-Performant SpMM on Arm SME" (2511.08158). None mentions cryptography, bitwise/rotate kernels, or constant-time execution.
- Conference/venue searches for SME or streaming-SVE + AES/ChaCha/Salsa/symmetric cipher, 2024–2026: nothing.
- tzakharko/m4-sme-exploration (the definitive M4 SME reverse-engineering effort): explicitly contains no cryptography discussion.
- Hello SME documentation (Jena) and mod_poppo's SME article (zenn): matrix multiplication only; I fetched the latter and confirmed no cipher, no XAR, no benchmarks.
- corsix/amx and Asahi Linux M4 feature-support docs: AMX is undocumented and reportedly gone/disabled on M4 in favour of SME; Asahi notes SME will be supported because it is standard. No crypto.
- Blog/implementer searches (Dolbeau, SUPERCOP, general "streaming SVE ChaCha"): nothing on Apple SME.
- Searches for anyone publishing that streaming-SVE and NEON run CONCURRENTLY on Apple cores for a throughput gain: NOTHING FOUND for any workload, crypto or otherwise.

FOUND, AND IT NARROWS THE CLAIM:
- Dolbeau's SUPERCOP `chacha20/dolbeau/arm-sve` means "ChaCha20 on ARM scalable vectors" is NOT new. It is non-streaming SVE, VL-agnostic C intrinsics, and pre-XAR (3 instructions per rotate). No accompanying paper found.
- tzakharko already published that the M4 SME block is one shared unit per core cluster, that a single core can saturate it, and that it is disjoint from the NEON pipes. Given that, "SME threads plus NEON threads add throughput" is a corollary. Our co-scheduling result is a *quantification and tuning* contribution, not a discovery of the mechanism. Occamy (shared SIMD co-processor across cores) is prior art for the general pattern.
- XAR as the SVE2 rotate idiom is public folklore (zingaburga's widely-read SVE2 gist analyses XAR latency/throughput on Neoverse V2 vs V3). Using it for ChaCha is obvious to an implementer.

WHAT SURVIVES AS GENUINELY UNPUBLISHED:
(a) That Apple's streaming-SVE unit is usable at all for a bitwise/integer symmetric cipher, with a measured cost model: which instructions exist in streaming mode (XAR, EOR3, TBL, MUL/UMULH.d) and which do not (AESE, PMULL, RAX1 — no FEAT_SME_FA64), the 9.6 ns smstart/smstop cost, and the v8–v15 zeroing hazard. This last item is the practically important one and I found it written down nowhere.
(b) The 4.03x speedup with its causal decomposition into 2.15x lanes x 1.87x XAR.
(c) The SME+NEON co-scheduling sweep with the counter-intuitive optimum (2 SME threads best; 4 SME threads worse than 2).
(d) The constant-time characterization of streaming mode, including that MSR DIT works inside it.
(e) The negative results: ZA/SMOPA is 5–7x slower than scalar for 5x51 Curve25519 limbs, with the ZA readout (6.17 ns/row) identified as the specific cause; plus the ZA-spills-to-kernel-memory observation about machine_save_sme_context().

The negative results and the security/hazard analysis are, in my judgement, the most valuable and most clearly unpublished material — more so than the speedup, because a speedup gets superseded and a "here is exactly why the matrix unit cannot help elliptic-curve arithmetic, with numbers" does not.

=== 2. SERVER-BLIND DATA PLANE: NOT NOVEL. THIS IS A KNOWN COMPOSITION. ===

Every element is standard and published, and I could not find a single component that is new:
- Per-recipient envelope wrapping: RFC 9180 HPKE; the optimized form (mKEM) is Katsumata et al. ASIACRYPT 2020.
- Key-committing AEAD: Albertini et al. USENIX Security 2022, now tracked in draft-irtf-cfrg-aead-properties.
- Signed hash chain for rollback/equivocation detection: this is fork consistency, SUNDR OSDI 2004, refined by BFT2F, SPORC OSDI 2010, Caelus S&P 2015.
- Scoped blind indexes: IronCore Cloaked Search ships per-(tenant, index, field) keys — essentially our (tenant, label, key_epoch). MongoDB Queryable Encryption ships a stronger version in a mainstream database. BlindexTEE (arXiv 2411.02084) uses the exact term in current literature.
- Untrusted relay that orders and stores but cannot read: SPORC, and the whole CryptDB/Mylar lineage.

SPORC is the closest published ancestor of Blindplane's overall shape, and a reviewer will ask what we add over it. The honest answer is: modern primitives, a cleaner crate boundary, and a Rust implementation. That is engineering. There is no new primitive, no new security definition, no theorem, and no leakage analysis in the structured-encryption framework. Do not write a paper on this.

Two specific places where Blindplane is materially WEAKER than the literature, which should be fixed in the README regardless of any paper:
- The rollback claim. A per-client persisted head gives per-client rollback detection, not fork consistency. A malicious relay can equivocate between two clients indefinitely and neither detects it, because every signature it shows them is genuine. SUNDR/SPORC get more; Caelus shows how to get near-real-time verification from multiple client devices. The README currently reads as if the hash chain solves equivocation. It does not.
- The access graph is leaked. Signal's private group system (Chase-Perrin-Zaverucha, CCS 2020) shows this is a design gap, not an inherent cost of server-blind storage.

=== 3. DEPENDENCY GRAPH AS SECURITY BOUNDARY: THE WEAKEST OF THE THREE. ===

Published work on structural/compile-time enforcement of security properties is substantial and much stronger than what we have: Cocoon (OOPSLA 2024) and Filament (arXiv 2026) enforce Denning-style information flow control inside unmodified Rust with a stated adversary model and a semantic property; cap-std does capability-oriented std; Asterinas builds a small sound TCB by construction; and the software-architecture world has had dependency-conformance checking (ArchUnit, dependency-structure matrices, "fitness functions") for two decades.

Against that baseline, `cargo tree --edges normal | grep -v '^blindplane-'` is a lint, not a proof. It establishes the absence of a *crate name*, not the absence of a *capability*. It says nothing about a relay that exfiltrates ciphertext, nothing about a future commit adding the dependency back with a plausible justification, and nothing about the client side where all the keys actually live. It is a genuinely good engineering practice and a legitimate README claim — "verify it rather than believing it" is the right instinct — but it is not a research contribution and presenting it as one would invite an easy, embarrassing rejection.

If you ever wanted a real claim here, the shape would be: encode "cannot decrypt" as a type-level or effect-level capability that composes across crate boundaries, and state and argue a non-interference-flavoured property. That is a different, much larger project.

=== 4. IS THERE A PAPER? YES — ONE, NARROWLY SCOPED. ===

STRONGEST FRAMING (in preference order):

(A) "Cryptography on Apple's Streaming SVE: a characterization of what the M4's SME unit can and cannot do." A measurement-and-implementation paper. Positive result: ChaCha20 at 4x NEON via 512-bit lanes + XAR. Negative results: ZA/SMOPA is a 5–7x loss for Curve25519 and Poly1305, with the readout cost isolated as the cause; AESE/PMULL/RAX1 absent in streaming mode permanently excludes AES-GCM and Keccak. Systems result: SME+NEON co-scheduling, +57%, with the tuning curve. Security result: streaming-mode constant-time behaviour, DIT availability, the shared-cluster contention channel, and the ZA-to-kernel-memory spill. This framing is honest, hard to attack on novelty, and the negative results are what make it useful rather than ephemeral.

(B) The sharper, higher-risk alternative: make the shared-SME cross-core contention channel the paper. If a process on a sibling P-core can reliably detect another process entering streaming mode, that is a security finding on a shipping consumer platform, and it lands at a security venue rather than an implementation one. It is also much less work than a full cipher implementation. Right now it is asserted, not measured.

VENUE: IACR ePrint immediately (it costs nothing and establishes priority, which matters given ePrint 2026/093 shows a group actively working the same hardware). Then Journal of Cryptographic Engineering, which is the natural home for implementation-and-characterization work and applies less novelty pressure than CHES/TCHES. CHES is reachable but riskier: reviewers there want either a record on a widely-available platform or a new side-channel, and "macOS-only, single-vendor, undocumented, Rust inline-asm" cuts against generality. If framing (B) works out, aim higher.

ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTS REQUIRED FOR CREDIBILITY — this is the real gap, and it is large:
1. A complete, test-vector-passing SSVE ChaCha20. Roadmap item #13 is still in progress; the 11.5 GB/s figure is a round-function microbenchmark, not a cipher. A paper cannot ship on a microbenchmark.
2. Full AEAD numbers. Poly1305 must stay in NEON (illegal inside streaming mode), so every chunk pays smstop/smstart. Measure real end-to-end ChaCha20-Poly1305 GB/s, not keystream.
3. Benchmark against the best available baseline, not our own NEON. ring and OpenSSL hand-written assembly, plus a port of Dolbeau's arm-sve code. "4x our own previous code" is not a result.
4. Cycles per byte at pinned frequency, with error bars, on an idle machine. Current absolutes were taken on a loaded shared developer machine — the README says so, which is admirably honest and also disqualifying for publication.
5. More than one chip: M4, M4 Pro, M4 Max (different SME unit counts), and ideally a non-Apple SME2 part or Arm's FVP, to separate "Apple M4 microarchitecture" from "the SME ISA."
6. Energy per byte via powermetrics. Nobody has published SME energy figures for crypto, and on a laptop part perf/W is arguably the more interesting axis.
7. Real constant-time evidence: dudect or a Welch t-test over many samples, not a mean-timing spread of 0.8%. Ideally TIMECOP/ctgrind under emulation.
8. Actually measure the shared-SME contention channel in bit/s.
9. Move the lab code into the repository. It currently lives in a /private/tmp scratchpad directory, and several findings-file paths point there. For an artifact-evaluated venue this is fatal; fix it now before the directory is garbage-collected.
10. Extend to a second primitive to show the technique generalizes: BLAKE2b or Argon2id's G function on .d lanes are the natural targets, and confirming RAX1's absence forecloses Keccak, which is itself worth stating.

=== 5. WHAT REVIEWERS WILL ATTACK — WEAKEST CLAIMS, RANKED ===

1. "Aiming to be the fastest constant-time implementation available." The measured reality is that most primitives are BEHIND ring (ChaCha20-Poly1305 0.83x, Ed25519 verify 0.75x, SHA-256 0.86x, AES-GCM 0.95x, Argon2id 0.9x). Only X25519 is ahead. This framing is indefensible and should be dropped from any write-up.
2. Rolling your own X25519, Ed25519, AES-GCM and HPKE, unaudited, in 2026. The assurance bar is now formally verified implementations (HACL*, fiat-crypto, Jasmin/libjade) and audited ones (ring, dalek). Reviewers and practitioners will read "zero third-party runtime dependencies" as a *reduction* in assurance dressed as a feature. The README's own status disclaimer concedes this. Note: I did not run a fresh search on the formal-verification baseline in this session; those citations come from background knowledge and should be verified before use.
3. The headline SME number is a keystream microbenchmark, not a cipher, not an AEAD, and the implementation is unfinished.
4. The 4x is against our own NEON rather than the best available baseline.
5. The +57% co-scheduling result: architecturally unsurprising once tzakharko's shared-cluster finding is known; it decays from 4x to ~1.1x by 9–10 threads; the optimal split is chip-specific; and it is measured on the round function.
6. Constant-time claims rest on mean-timing spreads (0.8%, 2.7%), which is not a constant-time argument, and PSTATE.DIT — the one thing Apple actually documents for this purpose — is not set anywhere in the crate.
7. The shared-SME unit creates an SMT-like cross-core contention channel. Our own findings file identifies this. It cuts against the security story of the entire library and is currently unmeasured.
8. Blind index leakage: equality and frequency within a scope is precisely what leakage-abuse attacks against property-preserving encryption consume (the CryptDB/Mylar lineage was broken this way). Naming the leaks is not bounding them; there is no leakage function, no STE-framework definition, no proof.
9. Rollback detection is weaker than fork consistency and the README overstates it (see section 2).
10. Dependency-graph enforcement is a CI grep with no threat model and no formal property (see section 3).
11. Reproducibility: absolutes on a loaded machine, lab code outside the repo, no error bars, no pinned frequencies.
12. Generality: M4-only, macOS-only, `core::arch::asm!` only because Rust has no SME/SVE intrinsics, on an ISA extension Apple does not document and whose SVL it could change.

=== IRRELEVANT / DEAD ENDS ===

ePrint 2025/2208 (ML-DSA on SVE2) — same authors as 2026/093, PQC only, useful only as evidence of what the SVE2-crypto literature consists of. Numerous ARM SVE HPC papers (Grace, A64FX sorting, "SVE Unleashed") — no crypto content. "Comparative Analysis of AES, Blowfish, Twofish, Salsa20, ChaCha20" (arXiv 2407.16274) — survey-grade, no implementation relevance. Searches for "Verdict" as a fork-consistency system returned nothing; I believe that name was a misremembering, and the correct set is SUNDR / BFT2F / SPORC / Caelus / Depot. Intel AMX + AVX-512 concurrency searches returned no published co-scheduling study for crypto either, which weakly supports the co-scheduling novelty claim but on a different platform. I did not search Google Scholar or DBLP directly (no access in this session), nor Japanese/Chinese-language venues beyond what surfaced incidentally — for a paper claiming absence of prior art, both are worth a manual pass, as is a direct check of the CHES 2025/2026 and SAC 2025 programmes.

papers.citation: Emil Lenngren, "AArch64 optimized implementation for X25519" (X25519-AArch64)
papers.core_idea: A scalar/NEON hybrid Montgomery ladder for AArch64 using radix 2^25.5 (alternating 25/26-bit limbs in 32-bit lanes). The A64 integer pipe and the NEON pipe each run an independent field-multiplication program; the two instruction streams are manually zipped so the in-order core dual-issues one A64 umaddl plus one NEON umlal every cycle, giving three 32x32->64 MACs per cycle. Field mul = 140 A64 instructions / 141 SIMD instructions; squaring = 99 / 98. The ladder avoids conditional swaps entirely: it computes A,B,C,D unconditionally and cselects (A,B) or (C,D) as the doubling input, because the addition formula is symmetric in the two terms.
papers.relevance: Two things transfer to us and one does not. (a) The cswap-elimination trick is representation-independent and drops 4 conditional swaps per ladder step from our montgomery.rs. (b) His section 4.1 is the definitive statement of WHY 2^25.5 was right there and is wrong for us: on Cortex-A53 UMULH has 1/3 throughput and plain 64x64->64 MUL takes a *data-dependent* 2 or 3 cycles, so 64-bit limbs are both slow and not constant-time. Apple cores have neither problem, which is why the 4x64 path wins on M4. (c) Do NOT copy the NEON hybrid; it is an in-order-core artifact.

papers.citation: Amin Abdulrahman, Hanno Becker, Matthias J. Kannwischer, Fabien Klein, "Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving" (SLOTHY)
papers.core_idea: SLOTHY is a constraint-solving superoptimizer (Google OR-Tools CP-SAT) that takes readable, de-interleaved assembly plus a microarchitecture model and automatically produces optimal instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining. Applied to X25519 on AArch64 with a 958-instruction loop body, using splitting/halving heuristics. Table 5: Lenngren handwritten 143,849 cycles (A55) / 144,168 (A53); their clean de-interleaved base 265,739 / 270,186; SLOTHY-optimized 139,752 / 140,096.
papers.relevance: This is the quantified answer to "how much is carry-chain scheduling worth": 265,739 -> 139,752 cycles, a 1.90x swing from scheduling and register allocation alone, with zero algorithmic change. Our Fe::mul is written as readable Rust and handed to LLVM; that is the "clean" column. SLOTHY is open source (MIT) and models AArch64+Neon; we could feed it a readable asm version of our ladder inner loop rather than hand-tuning. It is also the provenance of the code AWS shipped: s2n-bignum's curve25519_x25519 credits Lenngren + this paper.

papers.citation: lib25519 speed table (Daniel J. Bernstein et al.), measured against OpenSSL 4.0.1 and s2n-bignum commit fce78c7c
papers.core_idea: Interquartile-mean single-core cycle counts, overclocking disabled, for X25519 keygen/dh/batch and Ed25519 keygen/sign/verify/MSM across ~15 microarchitectures. ARM rows: Cortex-A76 X dh 111,516 (lib25519+s2n), 115,105 (lib25519), 111,541 (s2n-bignum); Ed sign 54,687; Ed verify 242,067; X key 49,165; Ed MSM 72,591. Neoverse N1 X dh 111,624, Ed verify 241,601. Cortex-A72 X dh 128,021, Ed verify 282,192, s2n-bignum 136,537. Cortex-A53 X dh 137,686. OpenSSL on the same ARM cores is 392,220-423,947 for X dh.
papers.relevance: This is the scoreboard we should be measuring against, and it is unflattering. Our benchmarks.md says X25519 = 27,798 ops/s on an M4; at 4.4 GHz that is ~158k cycles, i.e. we are SLOWER in cycles than a 2018 Cortex-A76 (111.5k) despite roughly 2x the per-cycle multiplier throughput. Ed25519 sign 61,989 ops/s = ~71k cycles vs A76's 54.7k. Only verify (~114k cycles) beats A76 (242k). It also shows the "X batch" column is flat on every ARM core (111,522 = 111,516) but 2.4-3.0x on AVX-512 x86 - the batching win is a vector-width win, not a batch-inversion win.

papers.citation: AWS Labs, s2n-bignum (arm/curve25519/curve25519_x25519.S, curve25519_x25519_alt.S, bignum_mul_p25519{,_alt}.S) with HOL Light proofs in arm/proofs/
papers.venue_year: Ongoing, AWS-LC component; used by AWS-LC and referenced by lib25519
papers.core_idea: Two AArch64 X25519 implementations. The non-alt one is derived from Lenngren + SLOTHY (scalar/NEON hybrid, radix 2^25.5). The _alt one is a pure scalar 4x64 radix-2^64 path: bignum_mul_p25519_alt is 20 MUL + 20 UMULH + 23 ADCS + 11 ADDS + 9 ADC ~= 100 instructions total; bignum_sqr_p25519_alt is 14 MUL + 14 UMULH ~= 78 instructions. Every function carries a machine-checked HOL Light proof of *functional correctness* against an idealized ARM machine model.
papers.relevance: The README benchmark on "a contemporary ARM platform" is the number that should change our roadmap: curve25519_x25519 = 26,661.8 ns (37,507 ops/s), curve25519_x25519_alt = 19,297.7 ns (51,820 ops/s). Our M4 X25519 is 35,970 ns. We are 1.86x slower in wall time than the 4x64 scalar path on an older ARM core. The README explicitly names the Apple M1 as the class of core where _alt wins because of "higher multiplier throughput". This is a directly portable reference implementation (Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0) and a correctness oracle.

papers.citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, Niels Duif, Tanja Lange, Peter Schwabe, Bo-Yin Yang, "High-speed high-security signatures"
papers.core_idea: The Ed25519 paper. Beyond the scheme, section 5 gives the batch-verification construction: pick independent uniform random 128-bit z_i, compute H_i = H(R_i,A_i,M_i), and check sum(z_i S_i mod l)B + sum(z_i R_i) + sum((z_i H_i mod l) A_i) = 0 as a single multi-scalar multiplication over 2n+1 scalars (half 253-bit, half 128-bit), using Bos-Coster (chosen over Pippenger because it fits in less storage). z_i are public, so no side-channel protection is needed inside the MSM. Also documents the radix-2^64 field representation and its carry-chain problem on Nehalem/Westmere.
papers.relevance: Quantifies batch verification exactly: single verify ~273k cycles vs <134,000 cycles/signature at batch 64 (2.04x), <125,000 at batch 128, <114,000 for larger batches still in L2 (~2.4x asymptote). Critically for us: "about 44,000 cycles on decompression" per signature, i.e. a third of batched verify cost is decompressing A and R. Since our recipients are long-lived, caching decompressed public keys is a bigger single lever than the MSM itself - the paper notes uncompressed input would drop batch-128 to ~81,000 cycles/sig, faster than signing.

papers.citation: Konstantinos Chalkias, Francois Garillot, Valeria Nikolaenko, "Taming the many EdDSAs"
papers.core_idea: Systematizes the divergence between Ed25519 implementations: cofactored vs cofactorless verification, small-order/mixed-order point handling, S canonicity, and non-canonical encodings. Shows that randomized batch verification is only sound with respect to the *cofactored* equation 8SB = 8R + 8H(R,A,M)A, so a batch that verifies can contain signatures a strict cofactorless single verifier rejects, and vice versa. Recommends the cofactored equation plus canonicity checks as the single form that is simultaneously batch-compatible and strongly binding.
papers.relevance: This is the security caveat we must state if we ship batch verification. Our edwards.rs has is_small_order and a "strict" verify path; strict/cofactorless verification is NOT batch-compatible. If we add verify_batch we have to either (a) adopt ZIP-215/cofactored semantics repo-wide so single and batch agree, or (b) document that batch is a fast pre-filter and every accepted batch is still bound by the cofactored equation only. Silent divergence between our own two verifiers would be a consensus-style bug in a data plane where the same record may be verified by two peers.

papers.citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, Bo-Yin Yang, "Fast constant-time gcd computation and modular inversion" (safegcd)
papers.core_idea: A constant-time divstep-based variant of Euclid's algorithm where each iteration depends only on the low bit of the running value and the sign of an auxiliary counter delta, so the iteration count is fixed and the control flow is data-independent. Inversion modulo 2^255-19 in under 4000 cycles on Intel Skylake. Later work (Wuille/Dettman/Maxwell, and the "More on safegcd" follow-up) reduces the divstep count to ~79.9% of the original.
papers.relevance: Our Fe::invert is Fermat: 254 squarings + 11 multiplications = ~265 field operations, which at our measured ~56 cycles/field-op is ~15k cycles, ~9-10% of every X25519 and every point compression. safegcd replaces that with a fixed-iteration bit-level loop. It is also the only inversion that stays fast when we cannot batch (single-record path). Formal-verification bonus: there is now a machine-checked safegcd implementation proof (arXiv 2507.17956), so adopting it does not cost credibility.

papers.citation: Boru Chen, Yingchen Wang, Pradyumna Shome, Christopher W. Fletcher, David Kohlbrenner, Riccardo Paccagnella, Daniel Genkin, "GoFetch: Breaking Constant-Time Cryptographic Implementations Using Data Memory-Dependent Prefetchers"
papers.core_idea: Apple M1/M2/M3 contain a data memory-dependent prefetcher (DMP) that dereferences values that look like pointers, leaking data-dependent memory addresses even from code with no secret-dependent branches or indices. Demonstrated end-to-end key extraction against constant-time OpenSSL Diffie-Hellman, Go RSA, Kyber and Dilithium. Setting PSTATE.DIT disables the DMP on M3 and later; it does not on M1/M2 (a HID chicken bit exists but needs kernel support macOS does not expose).
papers.relevance: Any claim that blindplane-crypto is "constant-time on Apple Silicon" is incomplete without this. Concrete actions: (1) set PSTATE.DIT (FEAT_DIT, Armv8.4, present on all M-series) on entry to every secret-handling primitive and restore on exit - precedent exists in Go issue 49702 and liboqs issue 1788; (2) state in the README that DIT closes the DMP channel on M3/M4 but not M1/M2; (3) avoid keeping secret field limbs in memory in patterns the DMP can mistake for pointers. This is a credibility item we can win cheaply because most Rust crypto crates have not done it.

papers.citation: Hwajeong Seo et al., "Optimized Montgomery Multiplication on Various 64-bit ARM Platforms"
papers.core_idea: Compares schoolbook and Karatsuba big-integer multiplication across ARM Cortex-A and Apple ARM64 cores. Finds that Karatsuba's advantage is entirely a function of the target's cycles-per-multiply-instruction: recent Apple cores have low multiply CPI, so the extra additions and subtractions Karatsuba introduces dominate, and plain schoolbook is faster there, while Karatsuba can still win on Cortex-A cores with expensive multiplies.
papers.relevance: Directly answers our question 3: do not implement Karatsuba for GF(2^255-19) on M4. At 4 or 5 limbs the recursion saves 1 of 16 (or ~4 of 25) products at the cost of several extra 256-bit add/sub chains, and on a core with two multiply pipes and 1-cycle accumulate forwarding the multiplier is not the bottleneck the adds are. Spend the effort on scheduling the schoolbook instead.

papers.citation: Oscar Reparaz, Josep Balasch, Ingrid Verbauwhede, "Dude, is my code constant time?" (dudect); Adam Langley, ctgrind; Peter Schwabe et al., TIMECOP (SUPERCOP)
papers.core_idea: Three cheap, practical constant-time testing routes. dudect: run the primitive on two input classes (fixed vs random secrets), collect timing samples, apply Welch's t-test with higher-order percentile cropping; no model of the CPU, purely statistical. ctgrind/TIMECOP: mark secret buffers as *uninitialized* via Valgrind memcheck client requests, so memcheck reports any branch on, or memory address derived from, secret data - a dynamic taint analysis for free.
papers.relevance: This is the lowest-cost credible artifact we can add. Practical constraint we must design around: Valgrind has no usable arm64 macOS port, so TIMECOP-style checking has to run on an aarch64 Linux CI runner, not on the dev M4. The macOS-native fallback is LLVM MemorySanitizer via -Zsanitizer=memory with unpoison/poison shims, which the CROCS ct-tools catalogue lists as a valid CT technique. dudect runs natively on M4 and is worth wiring into blindplane-bench.

papers.citation: Andres Erbsen, Jade Philipoom, Jason Gross, Robert Sloan, Adam Chlipala, "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic - With Proofs, Without Compromises" (fiat-crypto)
papers.core_idea: A Coq-verified compiler that generates field-arithmetic code (saturated 4x64 Solinas and unsaturated 5x51 forms for 2^255-19, plus the group order) from a high-level specification, with a machine-checked proof of functional correctness and bounds. The generated code is branch-free and index-free by construction, so the standard software constant-time property holds structurally rather than by testing. Deployed in BoringSSL, Go, Firefox.
papers.relevance: The cheapest path to a *machine-checked* claim for the field layer specifically. We could vendor fiat-generated curve25519_64 (5x51) or curve25519_solinas (4x64) as a `verified` feature and differential-test our hand-tuned Fe against it in CI: we then get a proof-backed reference plus a fast path, and can state honestly that the fast path is validated against Coq-proven code. It will not match hand-scheduled asm on speed, so it is a correctness artifact, not a performance one.

papers.citation: Jose Bacelar Almeida, Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe et al., Jasmin / libjade
papers.core_idea: Jasmin is an assembly-level programming language with predictable code generation, an EasyCrypt backend for proving functional correctness and cryptographic security, and a type system that proves constant-time (and speculative constant-time) properties of the generated assembly. libjade is the resulting library of verified high-speed primitives, benchmarked in SUPERCOP alongside hand assembly.
papers.relevance: This is the only ecosystem that gives assembly-grade speed *and* a machine-checked constant-time guarantee, which is exactly the combination blindplane claims. Realistic use: port only the ladder inner loop and Fe::mul/sqr to Jasmin, verify CT, and emit the asm we link into the crate - rather than rewriting the whole library. Compare honestly with s2n-bignum, whose README states its HOL Light proofs cover functional correctness only and that constant-time is "not actually rigorously machine-checked at present".

papers.citation: Antoine Geimer, Mathéo Vergnolle, Frédéric Recoules, Lesly-Ann Daniel, Sébastien Bardin, Clémentine Maurice, "A Systematic Evaluation of Automated Tools for Side-Channel Analysis of Cryptographic Libraries" / "A usability evaluation of constant-time analysis tools"; plus the CROCS ct-tools catalogue
papers.core_idea: Catalogues and empirically compares 34 constant-time analysis tools grouped as statistical (dudect, tlsfuzzer, Manifold), dynamic/instrumentation (ctgrind, TIMECOP, MemSan, Microwalk, DATA, Constantine, ct-fuzz), symbolic execution (Binsec/Rel, haybale-pitchfork, pitchfork-angr, tis-ct) and formal methods (ct-verif, FaCT, CT-WASM, Themis). Evaluates usability, false positives and required expertise.
papers.relevance: Use this as the menu when we write the "how we verify constant time" section of the README. Realistic tiering for a Rust crate: dudect natively on M4 -> TIMECOP/ctgrind on an aarch64 Linux CI runner -> haybale-pitchfork on LLVM IR for the scalar/field modules (it is the one symbolic tool that ingests what rustc emits) -> fiat-crypto differential tests for functional correctness. Binsec/Rel is binary-level but its maturity is on x86.

papers.citation: curve25519-dalek, backend/serial/scalar_mul/vartime_double_base.rs and curve_models
papers.core_idea: aA + bB is computed with interleaved w-NAF (Straus). The variable point A uses width-5 NAF with an 8-entry ProjectiveNiels table built per call; the basepoint B uses width-8 NAF against a static 64-entry AffineNiels table (AFFINE_ODD_MULTIPLES_OF_BASEPOINT) when the precomputed-tables feature is on. The accumulator lives in ProjectivePoint (no T coordinate), doubling produces a CompletedPoint, and .as_extended() (which materializes T) is paid only on iterations where an addition actually happens.
papers.relevance: This is precisely where our 0.75x comes from and it is a source-level fix. Our edwards.rs uses width-5 NAF for BOTH scalars and only an 8-entry basepoint table, and our accumulator is always a full EdwardsPoint whose double() spends 4S+4M because it recomputes T every iteration. Going to w=8 for b removes ~24 of ~43 basepoint additions (nonzero digit density drops from 1/6 to 1/9); adopting a T-free projective accumulator saves ~1 field multiplication on each of the ~200 iterations that have no addition. Together these are worth roughly 12-15% before any field-arithmetic work.

techniques.name: Switch GF(2^255-19) to 4x64 radix-2^64 with MUL/UMULH (keep 5x51 only as the portable fallback)
techniques.source: s2n-bignum bignum_mul_p25519_alt / curve25519_x25519_alt; Ed25519 paper radix-2^64 section; ePrint 2021/185
techniques.applies_to: field.rs Fe::mul, Fe::square, and therefore montgomery.rs (X25519) and edwards.rs (sign + verify)
techniques.expected_gain: Multiplier-throughput floor drops from 50 multiply uops per field mul (5x51: 25 MUL + 25 UMULH) to 40 (4x64: 20 MUL + 20 UMULH including the 38x fold-back), and for squaring from 30 to 28. With Firestorm-class cores having two integer multiply pipes, that is a floor of ~20 cycles vs ~25 cycles per multiplication. Measured end-to-end evidence: s2n-bignum's 4x64 _alt path is 1.38x faster than its own Lenngren/SLOTHY hybrid on a contemporary ARM core (19,297.7 ns vs 26,661.8 ns per X25519).
techniques.effort: Medium-high. ~2 weeks. The representation change touches every Fe consumer; the hard part is the ADCS carry chain, which is serial through the flags and needs care to interleave. s2n-bignum's Apache/ISC/MIT-0 source is a legal, readable reference and its HOL Light spec is a correctness oracle.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes on Apple cores, and this is the load-bearing caveat: 64x64 MUL is fixed-latency on Apple M-series, but Lenngren documents that on Cortex-A53/A55 plain MUL takes a data-dependent 2 or 3 cycles, so a 4x64 path is not constant-time there. Gate it behind an Apple/OoO-core cfg and keep 5x51 for A53/A55-class targets.

techniques.name: Fix Fe::mul scheduling before changing the radix - we are ~2.2x above our own representation's floor
techniques.source: SLOTHY (TCHES 2024) Table 5: 265,739 -> 139,752 cycles from scheduling alone; our own results/benchmarks.md
techniques.applies_to: field.rs (the u128 accumulate/carry code), montgomery.rs ladder
techniques.expected_gain: Our X25519 is 27,798 ops/s on M4 = ~158k cycles at 4.4 GHz. A ladder is 255 x (5M+4S+1 mul121666) plus a Fermat inversion (254S+11M) = ~2815 field operations, so we are at ~56 cycles per field operation. The 5x51 multiplier floor is ~25 cycles and the 24 accumulating 128-bit adds are ~12 cycles of ALU that should overlap. So ~2.0-2.2x is available in the existing representation. SLOTHY's own measurement of the same class of change was 1.90x.
techniques.effort: Medium. Start by hand-lowering the u128 accumulators to explicit (lo,hi) u64 pairs with umulh intrinsics so LLVM stops re-materializing 128-bit values, then check the asm for spills. If that plateaus, feed a readable asm version of the loop to SLOTHY (MIT-licensed, models AArch64+Neon).
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes - pure scheduling and register allocation, no data-dependent control flow introduced. Re-run the CT test suite afterwards because inline asm and intrinsics bypass whatever guarantees the current pure-Rust form gives.

techniques.name: Eliminate the per-step conditional swap in the Montgomery ladder
techniques.source: Lenngren X25519-AArch64, section 5 / Algorithm 1
techniques.applies_to: montgomery.rs
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified in isolation by the source, but it removes 4 constant-time cswaps (each 5 limb-wise mask/xor triples) per ladder step x 255 steps. The trick: the differential addition is symmetric in its two operands so it needs no swap at all; compute A,B,C,D unconditionally and cselect (A,B) or (C,D) only as the input to the doubling. Two cselects of two values instead of four cswaps of four values.
techniques.effort: Low. A day. Purely a restructuring of the ladder step.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes, and strictly better than what we have: fewer secret-dependent select operations, all still mask-based. Note the ladder's last processed bit is fixed to 0 by RFC 7748 clamping, so no final swap is needed either.

techniques.name: Width-8 NAF for the basepoint scalar in Ed25519 verification
techniques.source: curve25519-dalek vartime_double_base.rs (AFFINE_ODD_MULTIPLES_OF_BASEPOINT, non_adjacent_form(8))
techniques.applies_to: edwards.rs::vartime_double_scalar_mul_basepoint, scalar.rs::non_adjacent_form (currently hardcoded WIDTH=5)
techniques.expected_gain: Nonzero-digit density in w-NAF is 1/(w+1), so going w=5 -> w=8 for the public scalar b drops expected basepoint additions from ~43 to ~28 over 256 positions. At 7 field multiplications per affine-Niels mixed addition that is ~105 field multiplications out of ~2700, ~4%. Table cost: 64 AffineNiels entries instead of 8, ~6 KB, built once at startup - trivially cacheable since B is constant.
techniques.effort: Low. Parameterize non_adjacent_form over the width and extend basepoint_affine_odd_multiples from 8 to 64 entries.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Not applicable and that is fine - this is the variable-time verification path where both scalars are public (the signature's s and the hash-derived scalar). Keep it strictly separated from the constant-time signing path, which it already is.

techniques.name: T-free doubling: keep the verify accumulator in projective form and materialize T only when an addition follows
techniques.source: curve25519-dalek curve_models (ProjectivePoint / CompletedPoint / ExtendedPoint distinction), Hisil-Wong-Carter-Dawson extended coordinates
techniques.applies_to: edwards.rs::double and the vartime_double_scalar_mul_basepoint loop
techniques.expected_gain: Our double() is 4S + 4M because it always computes t = e*h. A projective doubling that skips T is 4S + 3M. With w=5/w=8 NAF, roughly 200 of 256 loop iterations perform no addition at all and therefore never need T. That is ~200 field multiplications out of ~2700, ~7%.
techniques.effort: Medium. ~3 days. Requires introducing ProjectivePoint and CompletedPoint types and routing the loop through them, matching dalek's curve_models structure. Also lets add_projective_niels return a CompletedPoint (3M to close) instead of a full extended point (4M).
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes - the coordinate-system choice is data-independent. It applies to the constant-time fixed-base path too, where it saves the same per-doubling multiplication.

techniques.name: Rebuild the constant-time basepoint table as affine-Niels instead of full Edwards points
techniques.source: curve25519-dalek EdwardsBasepointTable (LookupTable<AffineNielsPoint>); our own edwards.rs basepoint_table()
techniques.applies_to: edwards.rs::basepoint_table + the fixed-base scalar multiplication used by Ed25519 sign and X25519 keygen
techniques.expected_gain: Two effects. (a) Arithmetic: 64 generic 9-multiplication additions become 64 affine-Niels 7-multiplication mixed additions, saving ~128 field multiplications out of the ~600 in a fixed-base multiplication (~20%). (b) Cache: our table is 64 rows x 8 entries x 4 field elements = ~64 KB, and constant-time selection touches every entry in a row, so we stream 64 KB per signature. AffineNiels is 3 field elements, taking the table to ~48 KB, and dalek's 32-row radix-16 layout with 8 doublings takes it to ~24 KB. Our Ed25519 sign is ~71k cycles on M4 versus 54,687 on a Cortex-A76 in lib25519, so there is well over 1.5x here.
techniques.effort: Medium. ~3 days, and it composes with the T-free doubling change.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes provided select_signed keeps touching every entry in the selected row (it currently does). Shrinking the table also shrinks the DMP/GoFetch attack surface, since fewer secret-indexed cache lines are involved.

techniques.name: Cache decompressed Ed25519 public keys (and R) across verifications
techniques.source: Ed25519 paper: "about 44,000 cycles on decompression" out of <134,000 cycles/sig in batch mode
techniques.applies_to: edwards.rs point decompression, and the record-verification path in blindplane-core / blindplane-wire
techniques.expected_gain: Decompression is a sqrt via x^((p-5)/8), i.e. ~250 squarings + ~10 multiplications, ~260 field operations, comparable in cost to a whole quarter of a verify. Bernstein et al. measured it at ~33% of batched verification. In our protocol recipients are long-lived and one key verifies many records, so an LRU of decompressed EdwardsPoints keyed by the 32-byte encoding removes that cost entirely on the second and subsequent record from the same signer. R is per-signature and cannot be cached.
techniques.effort: Low. A day, plus a decision about cache scope and eviction. No cryptographic risk: public keys are public.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes - public keys are not secret, so a data-dependent cache is not a leak. Do keep the cache out of any code path handling secret keys.

techniques.name: Randomized batch verification with Bos-Coster multi-scalar multiplication
techniques.source: Ed25519 paper section 5; curve25519-dalek Straus/Pippenger MSM; "Taming the many EdDSAs" for the semantics
techniques.applies_to: A new verify_batch in edwards.rs + the record-open path (open, 4 KiB currently 17,264 ops/s)
techniques.expected_gain: Measured by the original authors: single verify ~273k cycles -> under 134,000 cycles/signature at batch 64 (2.04x), under 125,000 at batch 128, under 114,000 for larger batches still resident in L2 (~2.4x). Combined with cached decompressed keys the paper projects ~81,000 cycles/sig at batch 128 - faster than signing. Construction: uniform random 128-bit z_i, single MSM over 2n+1 scalars (n of 253 bits, n of 128 bits, one merged basepoint scalar).
techniques.effort: High. ~2 weeks. Needs a Bos-Coster heap MSM (or Straus for small n, Pippenger for large n - dalek switches between them at a few hundred terms), plus a fallback-to-individual path and an API that reports which signature failed.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Not applicable by design and that is correct: the z_i are public randomness, so the MSM needs no side-channel protection - the Ed25519 paper says this explicitly. The real caveat is semantic, not timing: batch verification only proves the *cofactored* equation 8SB = 8R + 8H*A. Per Chalkias-Garillot-Nikolaenko, a batch-accepted signature can be rejected by our current strict cofactorless verifier. Pick one semantics repo-wide (ZIP-215/cofactored) or document the divergence. Also: a failed batch tells you only that at least one signature is bad, so fall back to individual verification - which is also the right DoS posture.

techniques.name: Montgomery's batch inversion trick across independent records
techniques.source: Standard (Montgomery 1987); lib25519 exposes it as a first-class primitive, crypto_powbatch/inv25519
techniques.applies_to: Fe::invert call sites: X25519 output (montgomery.rs), point compression after fixed-base multiplication (Ed25519 sign), HPKE encapsulation
techniques.expected_gain: n inversions collapse to 1 inversion + 3(n-1) multiplications. Our Fermat inversion is ~265 field operations; batching 16 records takes the per-record inversion cost from ~265 to ~3 + 265/16 = ~20 field operations, i.e. ~245 field operations saved per record, roughly 9% of an X25519. Our seal-batch path already runs records independently across cores at 65,497 records/s, so the batching structure exists; it needs a phase split (all ladders -> one batched inversion -> all outputs).
techniques.effort: Medium. ~1 week. The awkward part is restructuring seal/open into two phases with a materialized intermediate, which costs memory proportional to batch size.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes, with one classic trap: if any element in the batch is zero the whole product is zero and the trick silently produces garbage. Handle it with a constant-time conditional substitution of 1 for zero inputs and a mask on the output, never with a branch.

techniques.name: Replace Fermat inversion with Bernstein-Yang safegcd
techniques.source: ePrint 2019/266 (safegcd), plus the reduced-divstep follow-up and the formally verified implementation (arXiv 2507.17956)
techniques.applies_to: field.rs Fe::invert, and scalar.rs if we ever need scalar inversion
techniques.expected_gain: Under 4000 cycles on Skylake for inversion mod 2^255-19, versus ~11-13k cycles for a well-tuned Fermat chain on the same core - roughly 3x. On our M4 numbers, Fermat inversion is ~265 field ops x ~56 cycles = ~15k cycles, ~9-10% of every X25519. Worth ~6-7% of X25519 standalone, and it is the fallback when there is only one record to process and batch inversion does not apply.
techniques.effort: Medium. ~1 week. The divstep loop is short but the constant-time transition-matrix bookkeeping is fiddly; libsecp256k1's implementation and the verified reference are good models.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes by construction - fixed iteration count, control flow depends only on the low bit and the sign of an auxiliary counter, both handled with masks. This is a strictly better CT story than a Fermat addition chain because there are no data-dependent squaring counts at all.

techniques.name: SME streaming-SVE batched X25519: 8 independent ladders in 512-bit lanes
techniques.source: Extrapolated from the lib25519 speed table's "X batch" column combined with our own measured SME facts
techniques.applies_to: A new batched X25519 path for the multi-record seal/open workload
techniques.expected_gain: lib25519's nPbatch (batch 16) costs 22,362-22,478 cycles per shared secret on Zen 4 and 21,666-21,678 on Tiger Lake, versus 53,572 and 64,604 for single dh - 2.4x and 3.0x. On Zen 3 and Skylake (no usable AVX-512) the gain collapses to 1.3-1.5x, and on every ARM core in the table (A76, N1, A72, A53) the batch column is *identical* to the single column: NEON's 128 bits is not wide enough to pay for it. That is the argument for SME: SVL=512 bits gives 8 u64 lanes, and we have already confirmed MUL and UMULH are available inside streaming mode (unlike AESE/PMULL). A 5x51 or 4x64 field representation vectorized 8-ways across independent ladders is the direct analogue of the AVX-512 win.
techniques.effort: High and speculative. ~3-4 weeks including a throwaway prototype. Do the prototype first: measure 8-lane vectorized Fe::mul throughput in streaming mode against 1-lane scalar, before committing. Our prior SME finding that ZA matrix tiles were a net loss for Curve25519 limb arithmetic does not rule this out - this uses streaming-SVE vector lanes, not the ZA outer-product tiles.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Requires care but is achievable: the batch shape is naturally uniform (every lane runs the same 255 ladder steps), conditional swaps become lane-wise mask selects, and there are no table lookups. Two things to verify: that streaming-mode MUL/UMULH are fixed-latency, and how PSTATE.DIT interacts with streaming SVE - undocumented as far as I found, so measure it.

techniques.name: Set PSTATE.DIT at every secret-handling entry point
techniques.source: FEAT_DIT (Armv8.4-A); GoFetch (USENIX Security 2024); precedent in golang/go issue 49702 and open-quantum-safe/liboqs issue 1788
techniques.applies_to: Crate-level: a guard type wrapping X25519, Ed25519 sign, AEAD key schedule, Argon2id, HPKE
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified as a speed change (expected to be near-zero cost - it is a PSTATE bit set and restored around a call). The gain is in the security claim: DIT gives an architectural guarantee that the defined set of data-processing instructions is data-value-timing-invariant, and on M3 and later it also disables the data memory-dependent prefetcher that GoFetch exploits. On M1/M2 it does not disable the DMP, so the README must say so.
techniques.effort: Low. A day or two. `msr DIT, #1` / restore in inline asm, behind a runtime HWCAP2_DIT / sysctl check, wrapped in a Drop guard.
techniques.constant_time_safe: This is the technique that makes the constant-time claim defensible on this hardware rather than aspirational. It does not fix everything - GoFetch on M1/M2 remains open, and DIT covers only an architecturally defined instruction subset, not caches or the DMP.

techniques.name: Three-tier constant-time verification pipeline (dudect -> TIMECOP on aarch64 Linux CI -> fiat-crypto differential)
techniques.source: dudect (DATE 2017); ctgrind/TIMECOP; fiat-crypto (S&P 2019); CROCS ct-tools catalogue; ePrint 2024/2060 usability evaluation
techniques.applies_to: CI for the whole crate; fiat differential specifically for field.rs and scalar.rs
techniques.expected_gain: Not a speed technique - this is the credibility deliverable. Tier 1 dudect runs natively on M4 and catches gross data-dependent timing with Welch's t-test. Tier 2 TIMECOP/ctgrind (Valgrind memcheck client requests marking secrets uninitialized) gives dynamic taint tracking that flags any branch or address derived from a secret; note Valgrind has no usable arm64 macOS port, so this must run on an aarch64 Linux CI runner, with LLVM MemorySanitizer as the macOS-native fallback. Tier 3 differential-test our hand-tuned Fe against Coq-proven fiat-crypto output.
techniques.effort: Low to medium. ~1 week for all three. The aarch64 Linux runner is the main infrastructure cost.
techniques.constant_time_safe: These verify the property rather than provide it. Be precise about what each buys: dudect is statistical evidence, not proof; TIMECOP proves the absence of secret-dependent branches and addresses along the paths actually executed; neither says anything about microarchitectural channels like the DMP.

techniques.name: Port only the ladder inner loop and Fe::mul/sqr to Jasmin for a machine-checked constant-time guarantee
techniques.source: Jasmin / libjade (CCS 2017, CCS 2020); contrasted with s2n-bignum's HOL Light proofs
techniques.applies_to: field.rs multiply/square and montgomery.rs ladder step - the ~10% of the code that is 90% of the secret-dependent work
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified as a speed change; Jasmin targets assembly-grade performance so it should be neutral to positive versus what LLVM currently emits. What it buys is the claim: functional correctness in EasyCrypt plus a type-system proof of constant-time (and speculative constant-time) for the emitted assembly. No mainstream Rust crypto crate has this. s2n-bignum, the closest comparable, machine-checks functional correctness only and its own README says constant-time is "not actually rigorously machine-checked at present".
techniques.effort: High. ~4-6 weeks including learning the toolchain. Only worth it after the performance work lands, and only for the primitives we would otherwise be hand-writing in asm anyway.
techniques.constant_time_safe: This is the strongest software-level guarantee available. It still does not cover hardware channels - Jasmin's speculative-CT extension covers Spectre-v1-style leakage but nothing proves anything about Apple's DMP, so the GoFetch/DIT caveat survives independently.

notes:
HEADLINE FINDING, and it contradicts the framing in the brief. The brief says X25519 is 1.4-1.6x faster than x25519-dalek; the repo's own /Users/serhiirihgt/dev/blindplane/results/benchmarks.md records 27,798 vs 24,045 ops/s = 1.16x. Either way, dalek is the wrong yardstick. Against the actual state of the art we are far behind: 27,798 ops/s is 35,970 ns per X25519, while s2n-bignum's curve25519_x25519_alt runs in 19,297.7 ns on an *older, slower* ARM core (the s2n-bignum README's "contemporary ARM platform" example). In cycles at 4.4 GHz we are at ~158k cycles, versus 111,516 measured on a 2018 Cortex-A76 in the lib25519 table. Same story for signing: our ~71k cycles versus 54,687 on that A76. So on X25519 and Ed25519 sign we are roughly 1.9-2.5x off the record on hardware that should be roughly 2x better per cycle. Only Ed25519 verify (~114k cycles vs A76's 242k) looks good in absolute terms, and that is the one the brief flags as weak because it is compared against dalek. I would recheck the M4 clock assumption (I used 4.4 GHz P-core) and re-measure on an idle machine before publishing any of these ratios, but the wall-clock comparison against s2n-bignum needs no clock assumption at all and is the one I trust.

WHERE THE TIME IS GOING. A ladder plus Fermat inversion is ~2815 field operations. 158k cycles / 2815 = ~56 cycles per field operation. The multiplier-throughput floor for our 5x51 representation on a two-multiply-pipe Apple core is ~25 cycles (50 MUL/UMULH uops / 2 pipes), and for 4x64 it is ~20. So roughly 2.2x is available inside the representation we already have, before any radix change. That reorders the roadmap: fix codegen and scheduling of Fe::mul first (cheap, ~2.2x ceiling), then consider 4x64 (another ~1.25x on multiplier pressure), then the ladder-level and inversion items. Changing the radix first would be doing the harder work for the smaller win.

RADIX QUESTION, SETTLED. 5x51 vs 4x64 is entirely a property of the target core, and the two published data points agree. Lenngren documents (section 4.1) that on Cortex-A53 UMULH has 1/3 throughput and plain 64x64 MUL takes a *data-dependent* 2 or 3 cycles, so 64-bit limbs there are both slow and not constant-time - hence his radix 2^25.5 with a hand-zipped scalar/NEON hybrid. s2n-bignum's README says the opposite for Apple M1-class cores ("higher multiplier throughput"), and its measurements show 4x64 winning by 1.38x. Dougall Johnson's Firestorm tables confirm two integer multiply pipes and 1-cycle MADD accumulate forwarding. Conclusion for M4: pure scalar 4x64, no NEON in the ladder. The NEON hybrid is an in-order-little-core artifact and copying it would be a mistake.

DEAD END: KARATSUBA. ePrint 2021/185 tested exactly this across Cortex-A and Apple ARM64 and found schoolbook beats Karatsuba on Apple because the multiply CPI is low enough that Karatsuba's extra add/sub chains dominate. At 4-5 limbs there is almost nothing to save anyway. Do not spend time here.

DEAD END: BATCHING X25519 ON NEON. I went looking for a batch-inversion win in lib25519's nPbatch and found something different.
