The "X batch" column is 2.4x on Zen 4 and 3.0x on Tiger Lake (both AVX-512), but 1.3-1.5x on Zen 3 and Skylake, and *exactly equal to single* on Cortex-A76, Neoverse N1, Cortex-A72 and Cortex-A53. It is a vector-width win, not an algorithmic one, and 128-bit NEON is too narrow to pay for it. This is what makes the SME streaming-SVE proposal interesting rather than redundant: 512-bit SVL gives 8 u64 lanes, which is the AVX-512 shape, and we have already confirmed MUL/UMULH are available in streaming mode. It is the one genuinely novel opportunity in this sweep, and it should be prototyped before it is believed.

DEAD END: THE KUMMER LINE. I looked at it because the brief asked. Gaudry-Schost genus-2 Kummer surfaces and Bernstein-Chuengsatiansup-Lange-Schwabe "Kummer strikes back" give a naturally 4-way-vectorizable ladder that maps well onto SIMD - but they are a different curve with different keys and no X25519 interoperability. For a data plane that has to speak HPKE/RFC 9180 this is unusable. Noting it only so nobody re-derives the same conclusion.

WHAT I COULD NOT GET. eprint.iacr.org returns 403 to automated fetches, so I could not read the full text of ePrint 2021/185, 2019/266, 2020/1244 or 2024/2060 - those four are cited from abstracts, search results and secondary sources, and the specific numbers I quote from them (safegcd's <4000 Skylake cycles, the Karatsuba/Apple conclusion) should be confirmed against the PDFs before going into a README. Everything quoted from Lenngren, SLOTHY/TCHES 2024, the Ed25519 paper, the lib25519 speed table and the s2n-bignum sources came from the primary documents, which I downloaded and read. ePrint 2025/523 turned out to be a red herring for us - it is Lenngren's newer Cortex-M4/M33 work (X25519 in 441,116 cycles on M4, X448 in 2,273,479), a microcontroller paper with nothing that transfers to Apple Silicon.

ONE THING THE BRIEF DID NOT ASK ABOUT BUT SHOULD HAVE. GoFetch (USENIX Security 2024) demonstrates key extraction from constant-time code on M1/M2/M3 via the data memory-dependent prefetcher, and PSTATE.DIT only disables the DMP on M3 and later. A library whose pitch is "fastest constant-time implementation, targeting Apple Silicon" cannot ship without addressing this. Setting DIT at crypto entry points is a day of work and would put us ahead of most of the Rust crypto ecosystem on exactly the axis the project claims to care about.

SEQUENCING I WOULD RECOMMEND. (1) Fe::mul codegen and scheduling - largest single win, no representation change. (2) DIT guard - cheapest credibility win. (3) Verify path: w=8 basepoint NAF plus T-free projective accumulator plus cached decompressed keys - closes the 0.75x gap and then some. (4) AffineNiels constant-time basepoint table - fixes the surprisingly weak signing number. (5) safegcd inversion, then batch inversion across records. (6) 4x64 radix. (7) dudect + TIMECOP CI. (8) Batch verification, with the cofactored-semantics decision made explicitly first. (9) SME batched ladder prototype. Jasmin last, if at all, and only for the primitives we would otherwise hand-write in assembly.

papers.citation: Conrado P. L. Gouvêa and Julio López, "Implementing GCM on ARMv8"
papers.core_idea: The canonical ARMv8 GCM paper. Three findings matter: (a) on AArch64 they *abandoned* Karatsuba and used four PMULL/PMULL2 calls for the 128x128 product, because getting the upper half of a vector as a PMULL operand costs an EXT and EXT was more expensive than the PMULL Karatsuba saves (Alg. 3); (b) modular reduction is done with PMULL against the constant 0x87 rather than shift-and-xor (Alg. 5, 3 PMULL + 2 EXT); (c) "lazy reduction": unroll GHASH as Y = [X_i·H + X_{i-1}·H^2 + ... ] mod f(z) so there is ONE reduction per N blocks, with an eightfold unroll and all powers of H kept live in NEON registers. They also note AArch64's RBIT makes the reflection trick unnecessary. Measured on Apple A7: GCM auth-only 0.51 cpb, AES-128-CTR 1.21 cpb, AES-128-GCM AEAD 1.71 cpb.
papers.relevance: This is the paper our GHASH is a partial implementation of, and we got the most important half wrong. We precompute 8 powers of H (good) but `gf_mul` in aes.rs:162-204 performs a FULL reduction inside every single multiply, and `absorb_eight_vectors` (aes.rs:261-287) then XORs eight already-reduced products. That is 8 reductions per 8 blocks, i.e. we do not implement lazy/aggregated reduction at all despite the comment claiming we do. Fixing this is the single largest GHASH win available to us. The paper also gives the schoolbook-vs-Karatsuba tradeoff argument we should re-evaluate on Apple cores.

papers.citation: Vlad Krasnov (Cloudflare), "chacha20_poly1305_armv8.pl" — fused ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD for AArch64, shipped in BoringSSL and vendored by ring
papers.core_idea: A single-pass, software-pipelined AEAD kernel. ChaCha20 runs 5 blocks in parallel in NEON (4 in ld4r-transposed lane-major form + 1 in block-major form, `chacha_qr_x5`). Poly1305 runs in *scalar* GPRs, base 2^64, 3-limb accumulator (`poly_stage1/poly_stage2/poly_reduce_stage`), and one or two 16-byte Poly1305 blocks are interleaved into every ChaCha double-round (`&poly_add(); &poly_mul();` between `chacha_qr_x5("left")` and `chacha_qr_x5("right")`). The Poly1305 lags the ChaCha by one 256-byte iteration, so the data hashed is the previous iteration's ciphertext. Net effect: the MAC executes entirely in the integer pipes while the cipher saturates the vector pipes, and the data is touched once instead of twice.
papers.relevance: This is exactly what ring beats us with at 0.83x, and we do the opposite: aead.rs:216-232 calls `ChaCha20::apply_keystream` over the whole buffer and *then* `Poly1305::update` over the whole buffer — two full passes, no overlap, double the loads. Adopting the lagged interleave is the highest-value ChaCha20-Poly1305 change we can make, and it is worth more than any Poly1305 micro-optimisation, because a well-scheduled Poly1305 becomes free rather than merely cheaper.

papers.citation: Andy Polyakov (CRYPTOGAMS/OpenSSL), "ghashv8-armx.pl", "poly1305-armv8.pl", "chacha-armv8.pl"
papers.core_idea: ghashv8-armx.pl implements 4x aggregated reduction with Karatsuba where the *folded key halves are precomputed and stored in the table* (`Hhl`, `H34k`, `H56k` = "pack Karatsuba pre-processed"), so the middle Karatsuba term costs zero runtime EXT on the key side. Reduction is the two-phase 0xc2 form: 2 PMULL per aggregation group. Measured GHASH: Apple A7 0.58 cpb, Cortex-A57 0.73, Denver 0.51. poly1305-armv8.pl uses base 2^64 with a 3-limb accumulator and s1 = r1 + (r1>>2) for the scalar path, and base 2^26 only for the NEON path; header table gives Apple A7 IALU 1.86 cpb vs NEON 0.72 cpb. chacha-armv8.pl gives Apple A7 4xNEON+1xIALU = 2.72 cpb and 6xNEON+2xIALU = 1.60 cpb — the scalar lanes running alongside the vector lanes are worth 1.7x on Apple.
papers.relevance: Three direct hits. (1) Our Karatsuba recomputes the folded operands at runtime through GPR round-trips (`a_lo ^ a_hi` on u64 lane extracts, aes.rs:167-181) — the folded H powers should be precomputed once in `Ghash::new`. (2) Our Poly1305 uses 44-bit limbs and 9 u64xu64->u128 products (18 MUL/UMULH) per block; OpenSSL's AArch64 scalar path uses base 2^64 and 6 MUL + 4 UMULH = 10 multiply-class instructions. We are doing 1.8x the multiply work for no reason. (3) Our ChaCha20 is 8 NEON blocks with zero scalar lanes; the published Apple-core record structure mixes IALU blocks in.

papers.citation: Samuel Lee / Fangming Fang / Xiaokang Qian (Arm), AArch64cryptolib and OpenSSL "aes-gcm-armv8_64.pl" / "aes-gcm-armv8-unroll8_64.pl"
papers.core_idea: The current state of the art for AES-GCM on AArch64: a single merged kernel that software-pipelines CTR-block generation, AES rounds, and GHASH of the *previous* group, with a MODULO (single reduction) block at the end of each 4- or 8-block group. unroll8 additionally uses EOR3 (FEAT_SHA3) to collapse pairs of XORs. I counted the AES-256 encrypt main loop exactly: 112 AESE (8 blocks x 14 rounds), 26 carry-less multiplies (14 PMULL + 12 PMULL2), 20 EOR3, 8 EOR, 11 EXT, 8 REV64, 4 TRN1, 4 TRN2 per 128 bytes. That is 3 PMULL per block for the product plus 2 PMULL for one reduction per 8 blocks. Note REV64, not RBIT — the powers of H are stored pre-"twisted" so no per-block bit reflection is needed. Arm reports unroll8 + EOR3 is worth ~33% on Neoverse V1 and 20–30% on Apple M1 over the 4-block version.
papers.relevance: Gives us the exact target instruction budget. Our GHASH costs 6 PMULL per block (3 Karatsuba + 3 for the in-line reduction) = 48 carry-less multiplies per 128 bytes against their 26, plus 8 RBIT per 128 bytes that they do not pay at all, plus GPR round-trips they do not have. Also: our seal loop (aes.rs:421-454) GHASHes the same iteration's ciphertext rather than the previous iteration's, so the AES and GHASH phases cannot fully overlap.

papers.citation: Daniel Hu (Arm), "Optimize chacha20 on aarch64 by SVE2" — OpenSSL crypto/chacha/asm/chacha-armv8-sve.pl
papers.venue_year: OpenSSL PR #18522, merged 2022; still maintained in master 2026
papers.core_idea: The only production vector-length-agnostic ChaCha20. Two code paths: SVE (rotate by LSL/LSR/ORR, plus an indexed TBL constant for rot8) and SVE2 (single `xar Zd.s, Zn.s, Zm.s, #imm` fusing the XOR and the rotate). Crucially it carries a `mixin` flag: when there is at least one extra 64-byte block of work beyond a whole vector's worth, every SVE instruction in the round function is paired with the *scalar* A64 equivalent on GPRs (`.if mixin == 1 / add @sx[$x], @sx[$x], @sx[$y] / .endif`), so one additional ChaCha block runs in the integer pipes concurrently with SVL/32 blocks in the vector pipes. Dispatch is by `cntw` at runtime; SVE-without-SVE2 is only taken when veclen > 4 words.
papers.relevance: Directly applicable to our in-progress SME streaming-SVE ChaCha20 (task #13). Two things to steal: the mixin trick (SVL=512 gives us 16 blocks per pass; a 17th block in GPRs is nearly free because streaming mode does not restrict base A64 integer instructions), and the exact XAR-based round structure, which we already validated in svl_xar_probe.rs. It also confirms XAR is the right SVE2 rotate primitive rather than SHL/SRI pairs.

papers.citation: Iakov Polyak (Linaro), "POLY1305 ARMv8 SVE2 vector-length agnostic implementation" — OpenSSL crypto/poly1305/asm/poly1305-armv9-sve2.pl
papers.core_idea: The first and so far only vector-length-agnostic SVE2 Poly1305. Base 2^26 with 5 limbs held in even/odd lanes of 64-bit SVE elements, r^k powers computed for k = number of 64-bit lanes (cntd), evaluated with SVE2 widening multiply-accumulate UMULLB/UMULLT/UMLALB/UMLALT (85 UMLALB, 20 UMLALT, 15 UMULLB, 5 UMULLT in the source) and SHRNB for the narrowing carry chain; TBL is used to select the intermediate r-power for the tail. The author measured on Graviton4 (SVE VL=128) by differencing `openssl speed -evp ChaCha20-POLY1305` against `-evp ChaCha20` at 8192 bytes and normalising by measured clock: Poly1305 NEON 0.62 cpb, SVE2 0.66 cpb — SVE2 is 6% *slower* at 128-bit VL, and is gated behind OPENSSL_SVE2_POLY1305=1 and only selected at VL >= 256.
papers.relevance: This is the recipe for an SME/SSVE Poly1305 on our M4 at SVL=512 (8 x 64-bit lanes, so r^8 parallel-lane evaluation). I verified against LLVM's AArch64SVEInstrInfo.td that every instruction it needs — UMULLB, UMULLT, UMLALB, UMLALT, SHRNB, ADDHNB, TBL, ZIP1/2, TRN1 — sits under the `HasSVE2_or_SME` predicate, i.e. legal in streaming mode, unlike AESE and the 128-bit PMULL which need HasSVEAES + HasNonStreamingSVE_or_SSVE_AES. The Graviton4 data point is the cautionary half: the crossover is above 128-bit VL, so this is only worth doing at SVL=512 and only if we are not already fusing Poly1305 into ChaCha's integer pipes.

papers.citation: Dougall Johnson, Apple Firestorm/Icestorm instruction tables (applecpu)
papers.core_idea: Per-instruction latency/throughput/port measurements for Apple P-cores. The crypto-relevant entries: AESE latency 3, throughput 0.25 (4/cycle), ports u11-u14; AESE+AESMC fuse into one macro-op, also 0.25; PMULL and PMULL2 (1Q) latency 3, throughput 0.25, u11-u14; PMULL+EOR fuses into one macro-op at 0.25; EOR3, BCAX, XAR, RBIT all latency 2, throughput 0.25 on u11-u14. But SHA256H and SHA256H2 are latency [4;5], throughput **1**, on a **single** port u14; SHA256SU0 latency 2 / SHA256SU1 latency 3, throughput 1, also u14. SHA512H/H2 latency [2;3] but throughput **2** (one per two cycles) on u14. Integer: MUL and UMULH latency 3, throughput 0.5 (2/cycle) on u5/u6; ADCS/ADDS throughput 0.333 on u1-u3.
papers.relevance: This is what lets us compute real floors instead of guessing, and it settles two of the sweep's questions. (1) AES-GCM: the unroll8 loop's ~193 SIMD ops per 128 bytes at 4/cycle gives a ~48-cycle, ~0.38 cpb issue-bound floor on an Apple P-core; our extra 22 PMULL, 8 RBIT and the GPR round-trips in gf_mul account for roughly 15 cycles per 128 bytes on top of that. (2) SHA-256 is genuinely latency-bound but only by about 28%: see the multi-buffer technique below. It also tells us PMULL+EOR fusion means we should write GHASH accumulation as pmull-then-eor pairs rather than accumulating separately.

papers.citation: Amin Abdulrahman, Hanno Becker, Matthias J. Kannwischer, Fabien Klein, "Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving" (SLOTHY)
papers.core_idea: A constraint-solving superoptimiser for AArch64+Neon and Armv8.1-M+Helium that takes a readable, correctly-selected assembly kernel and automatically finds optimal instruction scheduling, register allocation and software-pipelined loop rotation against a microarchitecture model. Applied to NTTs for Kyber/Dilithium and to the X25519 scalar multiplication on Cortex-A55, matching or beating hand-tuned prior art while keeping the source auditable. The tool is open source and the microarchitecture models are user-extensible.
papers.relevance: Our three remaining deficits (AES-GCM 0.95x, ChaCha20-Poly1305 0.83x, SHA-256 0.86x) are all scheduling problems on kernels whose instruction selection is already right. SLOTHY is the mechanised way to close them without hand-writing thousands of lines of .S, and it is exactly the tool for the fused ChaCha+Poly1305 interleave, where the hard part is deciding where in the double-round to place each poly_mul stage. It needs an Apple P-core model, which we can build from the Firestorm tables above — that model does not exist publicly and would be a real contribution.

papers.citation: Mamone Tarsha Kurdi and Niels Möller, "Efficient GHASH and POLYVAL Implementation Using Polynomial Multiplication: Optimized 64-bit Decomposition with Bit-Reversal Elimination"
papers.core_idea: Computes the universal hash directly in the bit-reversed representation that carry-less multiply instructions natively produce, removing the reflection/bit-reversal step from the hot loop entirely, and decomposes the 128x128 product into 64-bit polynomial primitives chosen for superscalar issue. Reported: POWER9 0.34 cpb and Intel Comet Lake 0.33 cpb for GHASH (11–35% over OpenSSL), and they characterise the tradeoff as hardware carry-less multiply favouring their reduction/folding form by ~1.7x over Karatsuba while pure-software Karatsuba stays 1.4–1.6x ahead in the no-hardware case. (I could not retrieve the full PDF — eprint.iacr.org PDFs are behind a Cloudflare challenge from this environment — so the per-instruction details are from the abstract and secondary summaries and should be re-read before implementing.)
papers.relevance: The bit-reversal-elimination claim is the modern, principled version of the trick we are missing: we call vrbitq_u8 on every 16-byte block (aes.rs:208-210, called 8x in absorb_eight_vectors). OpenSSL/AArch64cryptolib avoid it by storing pre-twisted powers of H and using only REV64. Whether we adopt the OpenSSL twist or this paper's representation, the per-block RBIT must go.

papers.citation: Martin Goll and Shay Gueron, "Vectorization of ChaCha Stream Cipher" (ePrint 2013/759, ITNG 2014); and Goll–Gueron, "Vectorization of Poly1305 Message Authentication Code" (ITNG 2015)
papers.core_idea: The origin of the r^k parallel-lane Poly1305 evaluation used by every vectorised implementation since: to hash n blocks with an n-lane vector unit, precompute r, r^2, ..., r^n, split the message across lanes so lane i accumulates every n-th block, evaluate lane-wise Horner with r^n, and fold the lanes together only at the very end. The companion ChaCha paper establishes the block-parallel vectorisation and the finding that vectorisation only pays above ~128 bytes.
papers.relevance: Background for question 3. Combined with the OpenSSL data (A7 NEON 0.72 cpb vs IALU 1.86 cpb) it quantifies the ceiling of the vectorised route. But note the conclusion this sweep reached: on Apple cores with two 64-bit multiply pipes at 2 MUL/cycle, and with a fused AEAD where the vector pipes are already saturated by ChaCha, the *scalar* base-2^64 Poly1305 is the right choice and the r^k lane technique is only interesting for standalone Poly1305 or for an SSVE implementation at SVL=512.

papers.citation: Hanyu Wei, Wenqian Li, Shiyu Shen, Hao Yang, Yunlei Zhao, "Optimized Implementation of ML-KEM on ARMv9-A with SVE2 and SME"
papers.core_idea: The only cryptographic-implementation paper on ePrint that actually uses ARM SME. Targets ML-KEM on ARMv9-A, using SVE2 for the vector-friendly NTT and SME for the matrix-shaped parts.
papers.relevance: Answers question 5 with a negative result that is itself useful: as of this sweep there is **no published academic work on SME or streaming SVE applied to symmetric cryptography**. Searching ePrint for SME/SSVE + AES/ChaCha/Poly1305/SHA/GHASH returns nothing; SME appears only in PQC contexts. Our SME ChaCha20 work (task #13) is genuinely novel and is publishable as-is. It also confirms our earlier finding that ZA tiles are the wrong tool for limb arithmetic — this paper uses SME only where the workload is already a matrix product.

papers.citation: Taras Zakharko, "m4-sme-exploration" — reverse-engineered Apple M4 SME characterisation
papers.core_idea: Systematic microbenchmarking of M4's SME. Establishes SVL = 512 bits (64-byte vectors, 4096-byte ZA tile), and critically that there is **one SME block per CPU cluster** — a large one shared by the four P-cores and a smaller one shared by the six E-cores — not one per core. Also finds that plain SVE FMLA in streaming mode reaches only ~31 GFLOP/s FP32 while the SME-specific FMLA variant reaches ~250 GFLOP/s, i.e. ordinary SSVE vector arithmetic on M4 is not full-rate.
papers.relevance: Two consequences for task #13. First, the cluster-shared SME block is the structural explanation for our own measurement that 2 SME threads + 8 NEON threads was the optimum — more SME threads cannot help, and the code must be written so that SME is a second engine alongside NEON rather than a replacement. Second, the 31 vs 250 GFLOP/s gap is a warning that SSVE integer throughput on M4 may be well below one 512-bit op per cycle; our measured ~4x-NEON on the ChaCha round function should be re-derived as ops/cycle before we size the 16-block pass, because the mixin trick and the block count both depend on it.

papers.citation: "Bitslicing the AEGIS"
papers.core_idea: Observes that an AEGIS-128L state update applies one AES round to eight state blocks at once, so the parallelism needed to fill a bitsliced datapath is already inside a single update, and constructs a sliced representation that keeps the rest of the cipher cheap. Result: AEGIS-128L runs 2.5x fewer parallel AES rounds per byte than bitsliced AES-128-CTR, and the constant-time implementations beat side-channel-hardened alternatives on ARM, RISC-V and WebAssembly.
papers.relevance: Adjacent rather than core, but worth knowing: if the goal is "fastest constant-time AEAD on M4" rather than "fastest AES-GCM", AEGIS-128L on hardware AESE is roughly 2–3x cheaper per byte than AES-GCM because it needs no GF(2^128) multiply at all. We already expose an AEAD enum (aead.rs) with a code byte, so adding AEGIS-128L as a fourth suite is cheap and would give us a headline number nothing in ring can match.

papers.citation: Daniel J. Bernstein and Peter Schwabe, "NEON crypto"
papers.core_idea: The founding treatment of NEON for symmetric and asymmetric crypto: constant-time NEON Salsa20/ChaCha, Poly1305 with 26-bit limbs chosen so that 32x32->64 widening multiply-accumulate keeps intermediate values in lanes without reduction, and the general principle that limb radix should be chosen from the available multiplier width rather than from the field.
papers.relevance: The reason 26-bit limbs are correct for NEON Poly1305 (32x32->64 vmlal) and 2^64 limbs are correct for scalar AArch64 Poly1305 (64x64->128 via MUL+UMULH). Our 44-bit choice matches neither multiplier and is why we pay 18 multiply-class instructions per block instead of 10.

techniques.name: True aggregated (lazy) reduction — one GHASH reduction per 8 blocks instead of 8
techniques.source: Gouvêa–López CT-RSA 2015 §4.3 "lazy reduction"; OpenSSL aes-gcm-armv8-unroll8_64.pl MODULO block; ghashv8-armx.pl 4x aggregated reduction
techniques.applies_to: AES-256-GCM (crates/blindplane-crypto/src/aes.rs — gf_mul lines 162-204, absorb_eight_vectors 261-287, absorb_four_vectors 292-309)
techniques.expected_gain: Quantified by instruction count: OpenSSL's AES-256 unroll8 main loop uses exactly 26 carry-less multiplies per 128 bytes (14 PMULL + 12 PMULL2 = 8 blocks x 3 Karatsuba + 2 for one reduction). Ours uses 48 (8 blocks x [3 Karatsuba + 3 reduction]). At Firestorm's PMULL throughput of 4/cycle that is 22 surplus ops = ~5.5 cycles per 128 bytes, on a loop whose issue-bound floor is ~48 cycles — roughly 11% of AES-GCM on its own.
techniques.effort: Medium. Split gf_mul into `mul_unreduced(a,b) -> (lo,hi)` returning the 256-bit product, XOR the eight (lo,hi) pairs, and reduce once. The reduction itself should move to the two-phase 0xc2 form (2 PMULL) rather than our three-PMULL 0x87 fold. ~150 lines of intrinsics plus new tests against the existing NIST vectors.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — pure data-independent PMULL/EOR/EXT, no branches or table lookups introduced. Same operand-independent instruction stream as today.

techniques.name: Fuse ChaCha20 and Poly1305 into one lagged pass, Poly1305 in scalar GPRs
techniques.source: Krasnov, chacha20_poly1305_armv8.pl (BoringSSL/ring); the same structure as OpenSSL's stitched x86_64 AEAD
techniques.applies_to: ChaCha20-Poly1305 and XChaCha20-Poly1305 (aead.rs:216-232 chacha20poly1305_seal / 234-250 _open; chacha.rs NEON path; poly1305.rs)
techniques.expected_gain: Largest single win available. Today we run two full passes: ChaCha20 NEON over the whole buffer, then Poly1305 scalar over the whole buffer, so cost ≈ t_chacha + t_poly plus a second trip through L1/L2. Fused, Poly1305 executes in the integer pipes (u1-u6) while ChaCha saturates the vector pipes (u11-u14), so cost ≈ max(t_chacha, t_poly) + ε and the data is loaded once. If our split is roughly 1.0 cpb ChaCha + 0.7 cpb Poly1305, the fused form should land near 1.1–1.2 cpb rather than 1.7+, which would take us from 0.83x of ring to ahead of it. ring's own numbers on this kernel are the 0.83x we currently measure against.
techniques.effort: High. This is a scheduling problem, not an algorithm problem: emit one poly_add+poly_mul between the left and right halves of each ChaCha double-round, and lag the MAC one 256-byte iteration behind the cipher so it hashes already-produced ciphertext. Realistically needs hand-written .S or SLOTHY; Rust intrinsics will not give reliable interleaving because LLVM will sink the scalar chain. Budget a week.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes, and it slightly improves the story: the tag is computed over data already in registers, removing a separate secret-dependent-length pass. Care needed only in the tail handling, which must stay branch-free on secret data (it is length-dependent only, which is public).

techniques.name: Base 2^64 three-limb Poly1305 instead of 44-bit limbs
techniques.source: OpenSSL poly1305-armv8.pl scalar poly1305_blocks; ring's poly_stage1/2/reduce; Bernstein–Schwabe NEON crypto (radix-from-multiplier-width principle)
techniques.applies_to: Poly1305 (crates/blindplane-crypto/src/poly1305.rs — LIMB_MASK line 10, absorb lines 180-217)
techniques.expected_gain: Exactly quantified. Our absorb computes d0,d1,d2 as nine u64xu64->u128 products = 9 MUL + 9 UMULH = 18 multiply-class instructions per 16-byte block. The AArch64 base-2^64 form (h0,h1,h2 with h2 two bits, r0,r1, s1 = r1 + (r1>>2)) needs 6 MUL + 4 UMULH = 10 — the h2 products need no UMULH because h2 is 2 bits. At Firestorm's 2 multiplies/cycle that is 9 cycles/block vs 5 cycles/block of pure multiply issue, i.e. 0.56 cpb vs 0.31 cpb floor. Roughly a 1.8x reduction in the dominant instruction class.
techniques.effort: Low — this is one self-contained function plus the init/emit limb packing. ~80 lines. The existing RFC 8439 vectors, the wraparound vector and the streaming-consistency test in poly1305.rs cover it.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes. The reduction is the standard `and #3 / and #-4 / lsr #2 / adds/adcs` sequence — no branches, no secret-dependent shifts. Strictly better than today because it has fewer carry-propagation steps.

techniques.name: Precomputed folded Karatsuba keys ("packed Karatsuba pre-processing") and elimination of GPR round-trips
techniques.source: OpenSSL ghashv8-armx.pl (Hhl / H34k / H56k table entries)
techniques.applies_to: AES-256-GCM GHASH (aes.rs:162-181, Ghash::new 225-243)
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified in the sources, but structurally clear: our gf_mul extracts all four 64-bit halves with vgetq_lane_u64 and XORs them in general-purpose registers (`a_lo ^ a_hi`, `b_lo ^ b_hi`). On Apple cores every SIMD->GPR move is a cross-domain op with multi-cycle latency, and there are four of them plus the return trip per multiply — up to 32 extra ops per 128 bytes. OpenSSL stores the folded key half once at init and folds only the data operand, with EXT+EOR staying in the vector domain. Expect several percent of AES-GCM, and it removes a class of scheduling hazard that also blocks the aggregated-reduction rewrite.
techniques.effort: Low. Store `powers_folded[i] = swap64(powers[i]) ^ powers[i]` in Ghash::new; in the hot path fold only the data with vextq_u8 + veorq_u8. ~40 lines.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — same operations, fewer of them, all data-independent.

techniques.name: Pre-twisted powers of H — delete the per-block RBIT
techniques.source: OpenSSL aes-gcm-armv8_64.pl ("twisted powers of H", REV64 only in the loop); Kurdi–Möller ePrint 2025/2171 generalises this as computing directly in bit-reversed representation
techniques.applies_to: AES-256-GCM GHASH (aes.rs reflect() lines 206-210, called 8x per iteration in absorb_eight_vectors and once per block elsewhere)
techniques.expected_gain: 8 RBIT per 128 bytes eliminated. RBIT is latency 2, throughput 0.25 on Firestorm, so ~2 cycles per 128 bytes on a ~48-cycle floor — about 4%. Small on its own but it is pure waste, and it frees issue slots on the same ports the PMULLs need.
techniques.effort: Medium — the fiddly part is getting the one-bit shift right when building the twisted H (OpenSSL's gcm_init_v8 does H<<1 with the carry folded through the 0xc2 constant). Must be validated against the existing NIST GCM test cases 13/14/16 already in aes.rs.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — representation change only, no data-dependent control flow.

techniques.name: Two-way multi-buffer SHA-256
techniques.source: Derived from the Apple Firestorm instruction tables (dougallj); the technique itself is Gueron–Krasnov "Simultaneous Hashing of Multiple Messages" and Intel's sha256-mb, for which no AArch64 equivalent exists in OpenSSL/BoringSSL
techniques.applies_to: SHA-256 (sha2.rs — hardware compress at lines 602-640; would need a new two-message API alongside Sha256)
techniques.expected_gain: Precisely bounded. Per 64-byte block, SHA-256 on ARMv8 needs 16 SHA256H + 16 SHA256H2 (four rounds per pair) + 12 SHA256SU0 + 12 SHA256SU1 = 56 instructions, all of which issue on the single port u14 at 1/cycle. Port floor = 56 cycles/block = 0.875 cpb. Dependency chain = 16 iterations x max(lat(SHA256H), lat(SHA256H2)) ≈ 16 x 4.5 = ~72 cycles = 1.125 cpb. So the latency bound is real but exceeds the port bound by only ~28%, leaving ~16 idle u14 slots per block. Interleaving two independent messages fills them exactly: 112 ops in ~112 cycles for 128 bytes = 0.875 cpb, a **1.28x throughput gain**. A third stream buys nothing — the port saturates at two. Contrast SHA-512, where SHA512H/H2 have throughput 2 on the same port: 40 SHA512H + 40 SHA512H2 at 2 cycles + 32 SHA512SU0 + 32 SHA512SU1 at 1 cycle = 224 cycles per 128-byte block = 1.75 cpb port floor against a ~120-cycle latency chain, i.e. already throughput-bound, which is why our SHA-512 is at parity and why multi-buffer would buy nothing there.
techniques.effort: Medium. Add a `Sha256x2` (or a `digest_many`) entry point that keeps two abcd/efgh register pairs and two schedules and emits the two instruction streams interleaved. Register budget is fine — 8 vectors of state and 8 of schedule per stream fits in 32. Only useful where callers actually have two independent messages: Merkle/hash-tree work, batch signature verification, HKDF-Expand of multiple labels. Not applicable to a single streaming hash.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — SHA-2 hardware instructions are inherently constant-time and interleaving does not introduce any data-dependent behaviour. Caveat: the API must not let callers accidentally leak which of the two buffers finished first via length-dependent tails; pad both to the same block count.

techniques.name: Scalar "mixin" lanes alongside vector ChaCha20
techniques.source: OpenSSL chacha-armv8-sve.pl `.if mixin == 1` scalar pairing; Polyakov's chacha-armv8.pl 4+1 and 6+2 code paths
techniques.applies_to: ChaCha20 standalone (chacha.rs NEON apply_keystream, lines 295-500) and the planned SME 16-block pass (task #13)
techniques.expected_gain: Polyakov's own header table on Apple A7: 4xNEON+1xIALU = 2.72 cpb, 6xNEON+2xIALU = 1.60 cpb — 1.7x from adding scalar lanes on an Apple core. Our NEON path runs 8 NEON blocks (two interleaved 4-block groups) with no scalar lane at all. For the SME path at SVL=512 the arithmetic is the same: 16 blocks in SSVE + 1 in GPRs is a free 6%, and the GPR block also covers the tail case for free.
techniques.effort: Low for the SME path (the mixin is literally one extra scalar op paired with each SSVE op, and streaming mode does not restrict base A64 integer instructions). Medium for the NEON path.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — ChaCha is ARX, identical operations in both domains, no branches. Important caveat: **do not do this and the fused Poly1305 at the same time**, because they contend for the same integer pipes. Choose scalar-ChaCha-lanes for standalone ChaCha20 and scalar-Poly1305 for the AEAD.

techniques.name: SVE2/SSVE Poly1305 with r^8 parallel lanes at SVL=512
techniques.source: OpenSSL poly1305-armv9-sve2.pl (Polyak, Linaro 2025); Goll–Gueron r^k lane technique
techniques.applies_to: Poly1305, SME streaming-mode path only
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified for M4, and the one published data point is discouraging: at VL=128 on Graviton4 the SVE2 version is 6% *slower* than NEON (0.66 vs 0.62 cpb) and OpenSSL ships it disabled below VL=256. At SVL=512 we get 8 x 64-bit lanes, so r^8 evaluation — nominally 8 blocks per Horner step against 1 for scalar. Whether that materialises depends entirely on SSVE integer throughput on M4, which the m4-sme-exploration data suggests may be well below one 512-bit op/cycle.
techniques.effort: High, and it should be gated behind a microbenchmark first. The cheap prerequisite experiment: confirm UMULLB/UMULLT/UMLALB/UMLALT/SHRNB actually execute in streaming mode on M4 and measure their throughput. I verified from LLVM's AArch64SVEInstrInfo.td that all of these sit under the `HasSVE2_or_SME` predicate (streaming-legal), unlike AESE and the 128-bit PMULL which require HasSVEAES + HasNonStreamingSVE_or_SSVE_AES — consistent with your existing measurement that AESE and PMULL are unavailable in streaming mode. That probe is an afternoon; the implementation is weeks.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes in principle — all lane-parallel arithmetic, TBL with public indices only. Watch the tail: OpenSSL selects the intermediate r-power via TBL with an index derived from the (public) remaining length, which is fine, but any hand-rolled variant must keep that index public.

techniques.name: Software-pipeline the AES-GCM loop: GHASH the previous group, not the current one
techniques.source: OpenSSL aes-gcm-armv8-unroll8_64.pl loop structure (PRE / interleaved CTR+AES+GHASH / MODULO, with GHASH block 8k+i overlapping AES block 8k+8+i); AArch64cryptolib "merged kernel" design
techniques.applies_to: AES-256-GCM (aes.rs seal lines 421-454 and the 4-block loop at 456-479; open at 522-562)
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified separately by the sources, but Arm attributes 20–30% on Apple M1 to the combined unroll8 + interleave + EOR3 change over the 4-block version. Our loop computes c0..c7 and then immediately calls absorb_eight_vectors on those same values, so the GHASH multiplies sit behind the full AES dependency chain of the same iteration. OpenSSL breaks that by hashing the previous iteration's ciphertext, so AESE and PMULL issue together and fill all four SIMD ports.
techniques.effort: Medium. Keep the previous iteration's eight ciphertext registers live and hash them during the current AES rounds; add a prologue and an epilogue ("PREPRETAIL"/"TAIL" in OpenSSL's terminology) for the first and last groups. Also worth doing in the same pass: replace the XOR trees in absorb_eight_vectors with EOR3 (we already detect FEAT_SHA3 for sha2.rs, so the feature gate exists), and rely on Firestorm's PMULL+EOR macro-op fusion by writing accumulate-into-the-product forms.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — pure reordering, no data-dependent branches. The open() path must keep its current behaviour of verifying the tag before releasing plaintext; the pipelining only affects the internal ordering.

techniques.name: Reconsider schoolbook (4 PMULL) versus Karatsuba (3 PMULL) on Apple cores specifically
techniques.source: Gouvêa–López CT-RSA 2015 §4.1 (they chose schoolbook with 4x PMULL2 on AArch64 to avoid EXT) versus OpenSSL/AArch64cryptolib (Karatsuba with precomputed folded keys); adjudicated with the Firestorm port data
techniques.applies_to: AES-256-GCM GHASH inner multiply
techniques.expected_gain: Small and needs measurement, but the arithmetic is worth checking. On Firestorm, PMULL, PMULL2, EXT and EOR all issue at 4/cycle on the same four ports, so what matters is total ops, not which ops. Karatsuba after key pre-folding still costs, per block, 3 PMULL + 1 EXT + 1 EOR to fold the data operand + 2 EOR post-processing ≈ 6 issue slots. Schoolbook costs 4 PMULL + 0 EXT + 1 EOR ≈ 5 slots, *if* both H^i and its 64-bit-swapped form are precomputed so PMULL2 can reach the cross terms without a runtime shuffle. That doubles the H-power register/table footprint (8 powers + 8 swapped), which is the reason OpenSSL did not do it — but we already burn 8 registers on powers, and the aggregated-reduction rewrite frees several temporaries.
techniques.effort: Low to test — the existing ghash_probe.rs harness in docs/research/lab/ is already set up for exactly this kind of A/B. Do it after the aggregated-reduction fix, not before, or the reduction cost will drown the signal.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes for both variants — no data-dependent behaviour either way.

techniques.name: Use SLOTHY with an Apple P-core model to schedule the fused kernels
techniques.source: Abdulrahman–Becker–Kannwischer–Klein, TCHES 2024(1) / ePrint 2022/1303; microarchitecture parameters from dougallj's Firestorm tables
techniques.applies_to: All four remaining deficits: the fused ChaCha20-Poly1305 interleave, the AES-GCM merged loop, the SHA-256 two-way multi-buffer, and the SME ChaCha round function
techniques.expected_gain: Unquantified for our kernels; the paper reports matching or beating hand-tuned prior art on NTTs and on X25519 for Cortex-A55 and Cortex-A72. The relevant point for us is that our remaining gaps are all scheduling, not instruction selection — the fused AEAD in particular has ~30 scalar Poly1305 instructions that must be threaded through ~150 NEON ChaCha instructions, which is precisely the search problem SLOTHY solves and precisely the problem LLVM will not solve from intrinsics.
techniques.effort: Medium up front (build and validate a Firestorm/M4 model — latencies, four SIMD ports u11-u14, the single crypto-hash port u14, two multiply pipes u5/u6, the AESE+AESMC and PMULL+EOR fusions), then cheap per kernel. The model itself does not exist publicly and would be worth releasing.
techniques.constant_time_safe: Yes — SLOTHY only reschedules and reallocates registers, it does not change the instruction sequence's data-dependence structure, and its output is auditable assembly rather than a black box. It preserves constant-time by construction as long as the input kernel is constant-time.

notes:
SOURCES I COULD NOT REACH. eprint.iacr.org serves its abstract pages fine but puts a Cloudflare interactive challenge in front of every .pdf from this environment, so I could not read the full text of 2025/2171 (GHASH bit-reversal elimination), 2019/842 (Improved SIMD Poly1305) or 2026/1338 (Bitslicing the AEGIS). Their abstracts and the OpenSSL/BoringSSL source I did read cover the techniques, but the exact instruction counts in 2025/2171 should be re-read before implementing anything from it — the cycles/byte figures I quote for it (POWER9 0.34, Comet Lake 0.33, the ~1.7x vs Karatsuba) come from the abstract and a search-engine summary, not from the paper body, and the 1.7x figure in particular reads like it may have been conflated with an unrelated Cortex-M4 result in the same summary. Treat it as a lead, not a number. Gouvêa–López I did extract in full and its numbers are first-hand.

THE THREE BUGS-BY-OMISSION IN OUR CODE, ranked. (1) crates/blindplane-crypto/src/aes.rs — the doc comment on Ghash claims aggregated reduction but gf_mul (lines 190-202) reduces inside every multiply, so absorb_eight_vectors performs eight reductions per eight blocks. 48 carry-less multiplies per 128 bytes against OpenSSL's 26, which I counted instruction-by-instruction out of the .L256_enc_main_loop body of aes-gcm-armv8-unroll8_64.pl. (2) aead.rs:216-232 runs ChaCha20 and Poly1305 as two sequential full passes; ring runs them as one fused lagged pass with Poly1305 in the integer pipes. That is the whole 0.83x. (3) poly1305.rs uses 44-bit limbs — nine u64xu64->u128 products, 18 multiply-class instructions per block — where every fast AArch64 implementation uses base 2^64 and 10. None of these is a correctness problem; the NIST and RFC 8439 vectors pass either way.

QUESTION 1, DIRECT ANSWER. There is no published technique beyond "8-block interleave + N powers of H + one reduction per N blocks + Karatsuba with pre-folded keys + pre-twisted (non-reflected) H + EOR3". That IS the state of the art, embodied in AArch64cryptolib and OpenSSL's unroll8, and Arm's own attempts to go further (unroll12, PR #27112) are microarchitecture-specific and only enabled for Neoverse N3/V3. The best implementations achieve 3 PMULL per block plus 2 PMULL per 8-block group, i.e. 3.25 carry-less multiplies per 16-byte block. Nobody beats "one reduction per N blocks" because at N=8 the reduction is already amortised to 6% of the multiply cost; the remaining floor is the 3 PMULL, and Karatsuba is already optimal there. The one genuinely open question is representation — 2025/2171's bit-reversal elimination — and that only removes fixed overhead, not multiplies. Shay Gueron's x86 canon (Gueron–Kounavis, "Intel carry-less multiplication instruction and its usage for computing the GCM mode") has no single ARM analogue paper; its ARM analogue is Gouvêa–López for the algorithms plus Samuel Lee's AArch64cryptolib for the scheduling.

QUESTION 1, THE FLOOR. Using dougallj's measured Firestorm tables (AESE 4/cycle on ports u11-u14 with AESE+AESMC macro-op fused; PMULL/PMULL2 4/cycle on the same ports; EOR3/EXT/RBIT 4/cycle; PMULL+EOR also fused), OpenSSL's AES-256-GCM unroll8 loop issues roughly 193 SIMD ops per 128 bytes: 112 AESE(+AESMC), 26 PMULL/PMULL2, 20 EOR3, 8 EOR, 11 EXT, 8 REV64, 8 TRN. At four ops per cycle that is ~48 cycles per 128 bytes = ~0.38 cycles/byte, or ~11 GB/s on an M4 P-core at 4.4 GHz. This ignores load/store pressure (16 vector accesses per iteration on 2-3 LSU ports, comfortably overlapped) and assumes perfect scheduling, so treat 0.4-0.45 cpb as the realistic ceiling. ring measured at 1 KB will be well above that because of per-call setup; the gap at 64 KB is the number that matters and is the one worth re-measuring on an idle machine. Our 0.95x-of-ring means we are close to ring, and ring is close to OpenSSL, so the remaining headroom is in the ~15 surplus cycles per 128 bytes I attribute above to reductions, RBIT and cross-domain moves.

QUESTION 2, WHAT I DID NOT FIND. There is no published cycles/byte record table for SVE or SSVE ChaCha20 — the OpenSSL SVE2 ChaCha PR (#18522) was merged with no benchmark data in the thread, and I could not find an independent measurement. The only VLA-crypto performance number anyone has published is the Poly1305 one from PR #28454 (Graviton4, VL=128: NEON 0.62 cpb, SVE2 0.66 cpb). So for ChaCha the published record on ARM remains Polyakov's NEON table (Apple A7: 1.60 cpb at 6xNEON+2xIALU). Our SME work has no published baseline to beat, which is both an opportunity and a reason to be rigorous about our own measurements.

QUESTION 5, DIRECT ANSWER. Nothing. I searched ePrint for SME, SSVE, streaming SVE, Scalable Matrix Extension, and each crossed with AES/ChaCha/Poly1305/SHA/GHASH/symmetric, plus arXiv and the general web for 2024-2026. The only cryptographic SME paper on ePrint is 2026/093 (ML-KEM on ARMv9-A with SVE2 and SME) and it is PQC, not symmetric. The only production SME/SSVE symmetric-crypto code anywhere is OpenSSL's SVE2 Poly1305 and SVE2 ChaCha, neither of which is SME-aware (both target non-streaming SVE2 and neither has been tuned for a shared-per-cluster SME block). Our task #13 is, as far as this sweep can tell, the first SME symmetric-cipher implementation. Two things to nail down before it ships: whether the SSVE integer op rate on M4 really supports the ~4x-NEON round-function figure when scaled to a full 16-block pass (the m4-sme-exploration FMLA data hints SSVE vector arithmetic is not full-rate), and the cluster-sharing constraint, which explains why your 2 SME + 8 NEON thread split was optimal and means the design must treat SME as a co-processor rather than a replacement for the NEON path.

ONE DEAD END WORTH RECORDING. I checked whether the SVE2 8-bit polynomial multiply (PMULLB .h) is streaming-legal on the theory that eight of them could synthesise a 64x64 carry-less multiply the way VMULL.P8 does on ARMv7 — it is under HasSVE2_or_SME, so it would execute. But that is 8 SSVE ops to replace 1 NEON PMULL, and NEON PMULL is already 4/cycle on Apple, so it loses badly. There is no path to GHASH inside streaming mode on M4. AES-GCM stays a NEON-only kernel; only ChaCha20-Poly1305 can use the SME engine, which is a good argument for keeping ChaCha20-Poly1305 as the preferred suite on Apple hardware despite AES-GCM being faster in raw single-thread terms.

ADJACENT FINDING, NOT ASKED FOR. If the objective is "fastest constant-time AEAD on M4" rather than "fastest AES-GCM", AEGIS-128L is the answer and it is not close: it needs no GF(2^128) multiply at all, just AES rounds, and ePrint 2026/1338 shows it needs 2.5x fewer AES rounds per byte than even bitsliced AES-128-CTR. On hardware AESE, AEGIS-128L should land near 0.15 cpb against AES-GCM's 0.38 floor. aead.rs already has an extensible suite enum with a wire code byte, so adding it is a contained change, and it would give the project a headline number that ring, libsodium and RustCrypto cannot match on any platform.
